TECH & BUSINESS

The great ticket wars have begun as BTS' ARMY in Singapore warm up their fast fingers in hopes of catching their favourites live after a gruelling seven-year wait. As one of the most anticipated live concert events of the year, fans are desperate to get their hands on tickets to one of the four nights of the BTS WORLD TOUR ‘ARIRANG’ IN SINGAPORE.

However, their enemies have also entered the battlefield: scalpers. Modern ticketing culture has seen the rapid rise of scalpers snatching tickets away from die-hard fans, using numerous bots to create fake accounts and bypass ticket purchase limits and queue numbers. The scalpers then upsell the tickets on reselling sites for ludicrous prices, luring fans who are desperate for a chance to catch their favourite act live.

As of today, 3 June, the ARMY membership presale has taken place. In order to buy tickets, fans were required to sign up for an ARMY MEMBERSHIP (GLOBAL) on Weverse to get the exclusive promo code. However, one fan took advantage of this, selling access to their code on Carousell for $20.

That's not all, others have even gone to lengths such as multiplying the original ticket prices up to a whopping 23 times when listing the tickets on the online reselling site StubHub. Originally, VIP tickets were priced at $388 on Ticketmaster, while on StubHub, they shot up to about $8,969, a significant jump from the originally listed prices.

Beyond Carousell and StubHub, one fan even took to X to promote the sale of the tickets she had scalped, with fans in the comments expressing their outrage. The tweet showed screenshots of a Google Sheet populated with rows and rows of available tickets, prices, and seat locations. Some of the tickets were bundled with seats positioned next to each other. ARMYs in the comments did not hold back, with some of them going on to comment things like, "@TicketmasterSG this person is a scalper who ruined so many real fans out of their tickets. Please invalidate their tickets" and "Can you handle this pls? This is unfair for the armys @TicketmasterSG @TicketmasterCS".

Ahead of today's ticket wars, Singapore Police Force (SPF) and Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) warned ARMYs about scams, advising them to only purchase tickets from authorised sellers. CASE president Melvin Yong cautioned fans that resold tickets may even be voided by ticket service providers. He added, "Purchasing tickets from unauthorised sources may therefore expose consumers not only to the risk of scams, but also the possibility of being denied entry to the event."

As excitement for BTS' long-awaited return to Singapore continues to reach fever pitch, fans are being urged to remain vigilant and exercise caution when purchasing tickets. While the battle for seats may be fierce, authorities and consumer groups alike stress that buying only through authorised channels remains the safest way to secure a place at the highly anticipated concerts. With additional presales and general sales still ahead, many ARMYs are hoping perseverance, rather than paying inflated resale prices, will be the key to seeing BTS live once again.

Feel the rush of music and be engulfed by the spectral soundscape created by the all-star lineup of the iHeartRadio Music Festival 2026. Featuring some of music's greatest talents, the two-day festival, taking place on 18 and 19 September at the T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, is set to be a celebration of culture, artistry, and fun.

 
 
 
 
 
View this post on Instagram
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

A post shared by iHeartRadio (@iheartradio)

The stacked roster features some era-defining names alongside rising stars who have been owning the charts as of late. Representing Asia on a global stage once more and reinforcing their legendary status as one of the greatest K-pop boy bands of all time is BTS. As they 'SWIM' through the overwhelming waves of success created by their comeback album ARIRANG, they return to festival stages once more.

Performing on night one, they are ready to deliver the same fiery passion and swagger that has defined their journey as one of the world's most notable K-pop idols. As of now, BTS are the only Asian artists featured on the list of artists performing, with more names set to be announced. The South Korean heavyweights claim their spot on the roster among some of the most legendary Western artists of all time.

IT’S OFFICIAL! BTS IS PERFORMING ON OUR STAGE THIS SEPTEMBER!

💜💜💜💜💜💜💜@BTS_twt @bts_bighit

More #iHeartFestival info: https://t.co/4lzimzHcfk pic.twitter.com/VAjlun6NzU

— iHeartRadio (@iHeartRadio) June 2, 2026

Also featured on the lineup for night one are the Goo Goo Dolls, with their soaring alternative rock and pop-infused melodies that bring a tidal wave of nostalgia with each verse. Keeping the energy high, Weezer switches up the vibes with a vast discography that spans pop-punk and rock-tinged rhythms. Adding another layer to the genre-blurring lineup is Cardi B, who is set to serve up top-tier rap verses and unbeatable lyricism as she spits some of her greatest hits on stage.

Get ready to sing every word with the crowd when @Weezer takes the stage at #iHeartFestival! 💙🎸

More show details: https://t.co/4lzimzHcfk pic.twitter.com/MSttqYHxxf

— iHeartRadio (@iHeartRadio) June 2, 2026

From there, whip out the cowboy hats and put the spurs on the cowboy boots to scoot and boogie to the country music charm of Kenny Chesney. Rounding things off, plunge into the 'Lush Life' and dance under the 'Midnight Sun' with Zara Larsson's perfect pop princess energy as she rocks the stage and commands the spotlight.

Hold on to the high of night one as night two presents an equally epic lineup. Have yourself a delicious scoop of the sweetest "Moonbeam Ice Cream" as Benson Boone blows the crowd away with his amazing vocal prowess and captivating stage presence before handing things over to country music royalty Lainey Wilson. Keeping the momentum going, Major Lazer will definitely give you something to 'Lean On' with their solid mix of EDM and dancehall beats, turning the arena into a full-fledged dance floor.

No chill allowed. Only ENERGY. @MAJORLAZER is coming to Vegas! 🔊🔥🌴

Get all the #iHeartFestival info you need to come join us in September: https://t.co/4lzimzHK4S pic.twitter.com/Kmy5a80pyO

— iHeartRadio (@iHeartRadio) June 2, 2026

Don't miss the unmistakable pull of Muse's rock versatility, which shines through in hits like 'Supermassive Black Hole', 'Uprising', 'Hysteria', and so many more. Slowing things down with effortless swagger, bask in the heat of Snoop Dogg's laid-back hip-hop legacy as he takes the stage and lays down beats that have defined generations.

West Coast legend incoming - @SnoopDogg is headed to the #iHeartFestival! 🐾😮‍💨🌴

Come party with us in Vegas this September: https://t.co/4lzimzHcfk pic.twitter.com/Cap3uUoFlT

— iHeartRadio (@iHeartRadio) June 2, 2026

With more artists yet to be announced, the lineup is already shaping up to be a combination of some of the greatest artists of our generation. Bringing together chart-topping superstars, genre-defining legends, and rising talents from across the musical spectrum, the festival promises two unforgettable nights packed with iconic performances and crowd-pleasing hits. Whether you're drawn to K-pop, rock, hip-hop, country, EDM, or pop, the iHeartRadio Music Festival 2026 is set to deliver a celebration of music that transcends genres and generations. Back in 2024, Anh trai ‘Say Hi’ commanded the spotlight with ease as the music reality TV show, created and produced by DatVietVAC Group Holdings, staged eight monumental concerts in Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, and two in Las Vegas.

In response to the incredible enthusiasm fans showed throughout the reality series, ANH TRAI "SAY HI" - DAY 9: REPLY 2024, which took place on 18 April at Vạn Phúc City, was a heartfelt thank-you to those who supported the show every step of the way. As the Vietnamese pop scene continues to grow, artists in that scene continue to branch out and evolve to put their region's greatest talents on the map, step onto global stages, and spread the joy that flows through their authentic artistry.

Background of the show

When the announcement for the anticipated ninth concert was first unveiled back in March by Vie Concerts fanpage on Threads, fans expressed their excitement, breaking records with the platform’s trending rankings rising to over two million mentions in the following 12 hours. This ninth show reignites the show's immense popularity as it has continued to smash ratings since its debut in 2024.

Anh trai ‘Say Hi’ translates to "Say Hi Never Say Goodbye" and it follows 30 musical talents who are referred to as brothers. In each episode, they participate in challenges and competitions to refine their artistry and become a member of the final band lineup that features the best contestants. Becoming an instant hit, the series has garnered over 18 billion views online, with many of its performances going viral across YouTube, Spotify, and iTunes, and sparking widespread conversation on social media.

Fans often showcased their unwavering support for participants and the show itself as they travelled from abroad to attend concerts and even organise fan events, building a positive and sizable fandom for the show. Due to the show becoming a cultural phenomenon, it quickly earned recognition from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism as a leading performance programme of 2024 and one of the Top 10 cultural, sports, and tourism events of the year.

The show's outstanding structure and wide reach earned it several awards, such as digital phenomenon of the year at the Vietnam iContent Awards 2024, Golden Apricot Blossom Award, Green Wave 2024, and the title of entertainment phenomenon of the year at Star of the Year 2024.

Gig report

28 of the 30 "brothers" transformed Vạn Phúc City into a high-octane celebration of Vietnamese pop and boundary-breaking musicality. Despite the absence of Anh Tú Atus and Quang Trung due to scheduling conflicts, the remaining talents turned up the heat, delivering the energetic performances the audience had been eagerly awaiting.

The members truly "Never Say Goodbye" as the show was packed with a nostalgic setlist of songs. They opened the concert with a heartfelt promise by performing 'Say Hi Never Say Goodbye.' The show unfolded with Live Stage one that saw the explosive renditions of songs such as 'Hút,' 'Don't Care,' 'Bảnh,' 'ICON,' and 'No Far, No Star.' Live Stage two, on the other hand, brought the vibrant soundscapes of 'You Had Me at Hello,' 'Poet,' 'Love Sand,' 'Halo,' and 'Catch Me If You Can.'

Rounding off the performances, Live Stage three took a more introspective turn with evocative lyrics and wistful melodies in songs like 'REGRET', 'Ngáo ngơ', and 'Cứ để anh ta rời đi'. Fan favourites such as 'The Minute and the Hour', along with performances of 'It’s All Yours', 'Sincere', and 'Walk', created memorable singalong moments for the audience.

Hai Dang Doo, NICKY, Song Luan, Gin Tuan Kiet, and Vu Thinh also brought an amusing twist to 'How to Love the Right Way', featured in You're Beautiful Say Hi. As the final beats of 'A-list Stars' and 'The Stars' reverberated through the venue, the show brought the journey full circle and left a lasting impression on the audience.

Although there was some controversy surrounding the slow ticket sales and changes to the stage location that were being discussed on social media, fans still undoubtedly had a blast during the show.

The overwhelming excitement from fans is a testament to the show's enduring impact, proving that its music, performances, and sense of community continue to resonate long after its original run. As the franchise prepares to return to the stage, the ninth concert promises to be another landmark moment in the ongoing success story of one of Vietnam's most influential entertainment phenomena.

Estudiantina of Melbourne – Ta Nisia [The Islands] (self-release, 2026)

Estudiantina Of Melbourne presents its second album, Ta Nisia (The Islands), an independently-released recording. The new work follows the ensemble’s debut, Journey to Rebetika, and arrives after two years of activity that included 26 concerts.

The new album reflects both continuity and change. The group’s music remains rooted in captivating smyrneika and rebetiko, taking the listener on a tour of joyful Greek taverns and nightclubs. At the same time, Ta Nisia also points to a broader musical direction. In turn, the title carries both a literal and symbolic meaning: each track stands on its own. Nevertheless, together, the pieces trace a larger story of migration, identity, growth, and belonging.

The lineup on the album features regular ensemble members Maria Antaras-Dalamagas on accordion and vocals; Vagelis Ginis on vocals; Camille El Feghali on kanun; Jenny Dixon on violin; Alex Petropoulos on guitar; Paul Karalis on bouzouki; Con Kalamaras on bouzouki and vocals; and Rosco Heck on percussion. Guest musicians Indra Buraczewska on double bass and Tim Meyen on cimbalom also appear on the release. Meyen’s instrument, a 145-string Austro-Hungarian cimbalom, adds an unusual, charming tonal element to the ensemble’s established sound.

At the same time, Ta Nisia reflects the cultural mix of Melbourne, where the group formed and developed its identity. 

Musicians: Alex Petropoulos on guitar, vocals, lavta; Camille El Feghali on kanun, zurna; Con Kalamaras on bouzouki, vocals, lavta; Jenny Dixon on violin; Maria AntarasonDalamagas on accordion, vocals; Paul Karalis on bouzouki, oud; Rosco Heck on percussion; Vagellis Ginis on vocals. Guest musicians: Indra Buraczewska on bass; and Tim Meyen on cimbalom.

Kieran McCoey, recording engineer. Recorded at 3MBS Studios Abbotsford Convent Melbourne 2025

items.body:
There is a moment on "Tea Horse Road," the album's fourth track, where the saxophone drops to a near whisper and the percussion seems to breathe rather than strike. You realize you are not listening to two musicians from opposite sides of the world so much as two people who have agreed, without a word, on exactly how much silence costs.

Lao Dan grew up in Northeastern China near the North Korean border. He showed enough early talent on saxophone and bamboo flute to earn a place at conservatory, then walked away from it. He studied dizi formally in Beijing and later at Shenyang Conservatory before turning toward avant-garde jazz and free improvisation around 2013. What he took from that training was not obedience. It was control: a deep physical understanding of breath through a tube, and an instinct for space that most Western free players spend decades trying to locate.

Barcelona-based Vasco Trilla came to the drums late, at nineteen, through progressive rock and metal. He worked his way outward through jazz, African music, and free improvisation. He has since appeared on more than a hundred recordings for labels including NoBusiness, Clean Feed, and Cuneiform. He plays like a man who understands that the wrong note at the right moment is still the wrong note.

The seven tracks here, from the opener "You Are You" through the closing "Nobodies Are Going to Sleep," feel less like a set list than a field journal. Lao Dan moves between tenor saxophone and dizi (Chinese flute), changing not just tone but altitude. Trilla generates rhythm without always generating a pulse, which is a different and harder skill. On "Fire Boy," Dan's flute cuts upward in tight spirals while Trilla accelerates with the controlled intensity of someone who knows exactly how hot to let things get. "Tea Horse Road," named for the ancient trade route connecting Yunnan to Tibet, sits at the emotional center. It is patient, unresolved, and genuinely rooted. The drummer shakes what sounds like a string of small cymbals while giving Dan a wide, open background. As the piece heats up, the intensity feels both grounded and spiritually convincing.

The closing track thins out slowly until you are not sure whether you are still listening or simply sitting in the room where the music happened. It is a good place to leave things.

You Are You; New Species 1; New Species 2; Tea Horse Road; Old Heaven Books; Fire Boy; Nobodies Are Going to Sleep.

items.body:
In this recording by bassist, composer and bandleader Ben Wolfe, titled Any Time After Now, there is a quiet assurance, with nothing straining for effect or feeling manufactured. Recorded in a single studio day alongside vibraphonist Joel Ross, pianist Sullivan Fortner, tenor saxophonist Chris Lewis and drummer Aaron Kimmel, the album spans ten tracks of original Wolfe compositions and exhibits a natural cohesion that reflects musicians deeply attuned to one another.

The opener, "Any Time After Now," swings with effortless authority. Wolfe's bass lines move with confidence beneath Lewis and Ross's contributions, while Fortner brings a strong rhythmic sense to the tune. Kimmel takes an imaginative turn on his kit, adding to the bebop narrative. "Waltz II" is striking for its delicacy. Buoyed by Wolfe's deep tone and steady beat, Ross and Fortner interact with arresting sensitivity, each phrase answered by the other.

"Blues" evokes a hazy, after-hours atmosphere. Lewis delivers an expressive performance, smoky, relaxed, and soulful. Ross follows with an improvisation rich in harmonic nuance, and Fortner settles into a blues statement grounded in groove and touch. "5/4 Groove" unfolds as Kimmel shapes the asymmetrical pulse with ease, while Fortner crafts an extended meditation brimming with momentum and tension. Wolfe's solo is a highlight, lyrical, poised, and deeply musical.

Wolfe, an unusual musician who associates music with color, shape and texture, writes compositions that carry visual weight. The music shifts between shadows, light, density and openness with remarkable fluidity. The result is a performance in which the band knows exactly how to inhabit these spaces.

"Down with Gravity" brings sharp angles and earthy funk. Wolfe and Kimmel work hand in glove, while Lewis stretches out with a harmonic vocabulary that yields clarity of ideas. There is a real bite here without sacrificing sophistication. "Always Four" opens with an assertive flourish from Kimmel, then settles into tightly focused exchanges between Ross and Fortner. Kimmel is back on board with crisp playing, taking the tune out as each idea feels purposeful.

"Til The Next Time" is a silky bossa nova that glides effortlessly into the ear. Ross, in full vibrato, phrases beautifully over Wolfe's subtle plucking. Fortner and Kimmel keep everything light and pleasant. The closing bonus track, "Green," swings with optimism and zest. Ross and Fortner carry the instrumental load with a keen sense of musical drama, while Wolfe and Kimmel deliver sharply etched pulses. The number offers a clear picture of Wolfe's melodic, thoughtful, and generous compositional voice.

Any Time After Now; Waltz II; If Only; Blues; 5/4 Groove; Do You Love?; Down with Gravity; Always Four; 'Till Next Time; Green.

items.body:
Storybook: The Music Of Mark Miller is at one level the unfolding narrative of its 10 musical selections. At another, it is a tale about its primary author, Mark Miller, who traced his journey from {jny: Racine}} to New York City with his previous release Mark Miller: The Return Of Slide Huxtable (Slide Huxtable, 2008)—a long road that is a serious jazz player's dream of making it in the Big Apple. But most of all, it is a compelling reminder to listeners everywhere that the Manhattan jazz experience is incomplete without a trip to hear the Birdland Big Band.

Birdland's original, long defunct basement club at "The Jazz Corner of the World" (Broadway and 52nd) now occupies a bigger mid-town area, bounded on the north by Jazz at Lincoln Center (60 St.) and, on the south, by the "new" Birdland (44th St). Start at 52nd St., walk 8 blocks in either direction, and you are there. But which direction? Is there a significant difference? Some observers have suggested that big band music from the north references the genius of Duke Ellington, whereas the sounds to the south are aligned with the swing of Count Basie. Yet "Storybook," the eponymous title of the album's Grammy-nominated first track, sounds like something else entirely.

Miller—much of whose "schooling" was on the road as trombonist-composer with the Minneapolis-based jazz group, The Motion Poets—has constructed a brilliant sonic gateway that owes as much to Bach and Bartok as to Ellington or Count Basie. Starting with a stately 3-note descending motif, the composition builds on that figure with rich harmonies and vibrant dynamics, answered by an ascending counter-melody played by the lower brass. Soon, the entire sequence is repeated, with the addition of creative commentary from Brandon Lee's flugelhorn. After a sharply articulated, vigorously syncopated version of the primary motif, Kenny Barron's infectious "Water Lily." Unlike earlier recorded versions that are slower and light-spirited, the tune here is taken at a driving tempo with accompaniment by piano and drums that borders on the intrusive (likely due to an over-hot audio mix-down). Besides an inventive piano solo by Kenny Ascher, the piece showcases the commanding artistry of saxophonist Troy Roberts, whose closing cadenza balances impressive pyrotechnics with satisfying musical taste. Next, the standard, "Tenderly," lightens the mood with a sprightly version of a waltz that, with the notable exception of Bill Evans' up-tempo version, usually receives the slow, pensive reading of Rosemary Clooney or the even slower 4/4 versions by Sara Vaughn and Billie Holiday. Miller's arrangement exhibits remarkable attention to detail, replete with spiraling flutes that simulate butterflies to complement the spring setting for vocalist Nicole Zuraitis. Brief solos by Sam Dillon (a. sax) and Raul Agraz (trpt) fit seamlessly with the colorful seasonal mix.

Miller's own "Chorale and Alleluia" is as contemplative and celebratory as its title might suggest. It features the percussive thunder of Chris Smith, who will also be critical to the driving samba rhythm of Chick Corea's "Spain." Tom Harrell's "Sail Away" is an inviting melody launched without affectation by Glenn Drewes' reassuring flugel. After band director David DeJesus' soprano sax has taken control of the cruise, Drews resumes his storytelling by, in effect, shutting off the engine (i.e., piano, bass, drums) and allowing only the sounds of wind and water for several choruses—the pulse of the band sans rhythm section.

It is tempting to continue with a play-by-play analysis if only to identify the soloists in an ensemble with no weak links. The Birdland Band is "deep" with talent, each player capable of assuming solo duties on any given night. Take, for example, "WTF," in which trombonist/composer Miller resumes the cruise with a witty trombone exchange between James Burton III and Sara Jacovino, one that recalls the musical conversations by J.J. Johnson and Jay and Kai Winding.

The last third of the program is cued up by the standard "Close Your Eyes," which opens with Zuraitis close to the mic as she fashions a soft, pitch-perfect, improvised chorus before yielding to an Ascher piano solo that swings with the sure-fingered authority of Wynton Kelly. Following a good-humored, equally swinging turn by bass trombonist, James Borowski, Zuraitis re-enters for an "out" chorus that soon becomes "far-out," her voice rising in pitch and volume to the level of a Maynard Ferguson set-closer. It works because the vocalist implants herself in the trumpet section, rising to a powerful climax as the job requires. Finally, we receive a healthy reminder that "swing" does not require a thing except a ride cymbal and a hi-hat. (If only audio engineers could figure out a way to include the shimmer of a Zildjian in their mastering of live sounds.)

Rodrigo de Arunez's "Concierto" and Corea's "Spain" are worthy additions to those already in print. And they are among the most "honest," avoiding orchestral instruments (French horns, double reeds, tympani, etc.) as well as electronic devices (Fender Rhodes, phaser boxes, onboard modulating effects). The result is a focus that remains fixed on the music, not the gear. And then there is the memorable close-out for "Spain"—an ascending Miller bass-line that, in effect, resolves a sparking, fractious debate between big band and drums, then between sections within the ensemble.

"The DoubleDown," the last track of the regular program, evokes a Sunday night gospel meeting with its inviting singalong melody in ¾. The primary preacher is Ron Wilkins, whose testifying on plunger-muted trombone produces a meditative bass solo by Noriko Ueda. But rather than exit quietly, the congregation is led back by saxophones to the main theme, then a sudden stop and lift to a new key for a final testament by Mark Miller's emphatic postlude on trombone.

Church is out, but the congregation's spirits crave more action. "Nonsense," an original shuffle-rhythm blues composed by Miller and Zuraitis, answers the need to sustain the sense of play embedded in every true storybook. Zuraitis delivers a nonsensical lyric in the strongest musical terms, conversing over stop-time chords with Miller's and Wilkins' vocal trombones. Next, she handles "vocalese" lines in tight unison with tricky instrumental figures. Finally, there is a vocal exchange, over pedal-tone bass, between the entire band and its girl singer, who has the last word: "Nonsense? Come on, whatever gets you.

Small wonder that, after hearing a call like that, visitors are setting aside Friday nights for a return to Birdland.

Storybook; Water Lily; Tenderly; Chorale And Alleluia; Sail Away; WTF;; Close Your Eyes;; Concierto De Aranjuez; Spain; The Doubledown; Nonsense;.

items.body:
At a time when economics often dictates the size and scope of a jazz group, adding a guitarist to a typical piano-bass-drums trio makes a world of difference. And when said guitarist is Peter Bernstein, the difference is even more pronounced. That gives bassist Harvie S a clear headstart on Bright Dawn, a modest studio date with Bernstein broadening the usual trio setting on the bassist's 21st recording as leader of his own ensemble—the first, however, following a 15-year hiatus.

The other members of Harvie's group, each of whom plays a pivotal role, are pianist Miki Hayama (Fender Rhodes on "Ghosts of Havana" and "Voice in the Sky") and drummer Matt Wilson who introduces and sparks the perky "I've Got Rhythm and Blues." That is one of Harvie's eight compositions, escorting Bob Dorough's playful "Devil May Care" and Chick Corea's sunny "Humpty Dumpty."

And therein lies the session's most problematic aspect. Even though decent and well-intentioned, Harvie's compositions are, to be frank, several lengthy strides away from memorable. While that may be traced in part to the group's makeup and Harvie S's resolve to lead the way, the fact remains that the success of any collective enterprise, regardless of size or shape, rests in large measure on its choice of material, and most of the songs on Bright Dawn simply don't measure up, even with Bernstein on board to help enliven them.

Harvie must be given props for naming one of his themes "Navalny" (and enhancing it with arco and string bass) but even that melody seems tame when compared to what comes next, the spunky "Rhythm and Blues," one of the session's few high spots. Hayama is an impressive soloist, as is Bernstein, and their expertise must be noted. That is not, however, nearly enough to raise Bright Dawn above the norm.

Ghosts of Havana; Devil May Care; Waltz for Vartan; Navalny; I've Got Rhythm and Blues; Yukimi's Song; Humpty Dumpty; The Truth; Voice in the Sky; Swithering.

items.body: Grief comes in multiple shapes and forms. None of them are pleasing to the eye or the ear. On 2:25, Alessandro Brivio confronts loss as a system under stress, short-circuiting in real time. The cover image—a specular photograph of graffiti spelling La Morte Non Ha Senso (Death Makes No Sense), doubled and inverted into near illegibility—sets the tone for a record that refuses clarity, mirroring the cognitive disarray of loss. Since his debut 6pezzi2009+lagodelnulla on Senufo, Brivio has explored loops and rhythmic repetition, often drawing from African patterns; here, those tendencies collapse inward, mutating into jammed circuits and malfunctioning systems. The opening track, “Cerchi” (26’03”), could stand alone as a release: an abrasive, confrontational expanse where different systems collide, forced through extreme processing and splintering into stuttering, unstable configurations. There are moments when the tension subsides, although the underlying rage keeps the momentum going. What once felt like carefully balanced studies now teeters on the edge of rupture, as if the material itself were resisting containment, at the risk of wearing itself out. Across the remaining tracks, Brivio sketches a fractured cartography of grief’s non-linear stages—denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance—without ever settling into them. “Diarismi” and “3.03” continue the tension between separation and collapse, their stratified layers suggesting a kind of sonic bargaining, each element vying for space yet never fully coalescing. It is midway through “Controra” that a fragile shift occurs: the density thins, and a subdued, almost hollowed atmosphere emerges, hinting at acceptance without fully embracing it. These quieter passages feel like depression folding back into reflection. The album closes with “VV,” a 21-second drift that exhales with no catharsis, no closure—only the faint release of pressure. Composed during a difficult period in 2025 as a tribute to a lost friend, 2:25 stands as a work of raw processing, where sound itself becomes both the site and the residue of mourning, revealing the process in all its necessary and inevitable messiness. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Air Signs rests at its distinct sound. Everything is pieced together very well, and all the noises, melodies, and synths are family—they all align track after track. Deschamps has a gift for cohesion. Even when he’s working with degraded loops, reversed recordings, and heavily processed guitar, nothing feels fragmented. Everything belongs. Dreamlike and reminiscent of ambient joy Air Signs by anthéne   Brad Deschamps has been quietly building one of the most consistent catalogs in contemporary ambient music. Working under the anthéne moniker, the Toronto-based musician has released extensively on Home Normal, Past Inside the Present, Whitelabrecs, and Constellation Tatsu, while also running the widely respected Polar Seas Recordings label. His collaborations with Ian Hawgood (as Rosales), Stijn Hüwels, and David Cordero have earned critical acclaim, and his solo work is known for its dusty, emotionally resonant guitar and synth-led compositions. Air Signs arrives on Dronarivm, a small independent label from the Netherlands focused on contemporary ambient, electroacoustic, and modern classical music. Each piece here feels very dreamlike and reminiscent of ambient joy. A very easy listen. Inspired by a hawk that landed right outside the window at Deschamps‘ workplace in a hectic area of downtown Toronto, the pieces are light and airy, reflecting the stillness of our natural surroundings in the midst of human-made chaos. Dronarivm has built a strong catalog over the years, releasing work from artists like Chihei Hatakeyama, bvdub, and o[rlawren], all mastered with care and presented in limited physical editions. “Starling” and “all a blur” are standouts here. “Starling” has such a beautiful build to it with subtle guitar noises. Deschamps processes his guitar loops with a Chase Bliss Lossy pedal and a Vongon Paragraphs filter, both creating unusual tones, overtones, and artifacts. He also makes heavy use of a Maneco 16 second delay for lo-fi forward and reversed loops. This approach to guitar processing is what sets Deschamps apart from more straightforward ambient guitarists—the loops are degraded, filtered, and stretched until they’re barely recognizable as guitar. Rather than letting the track fade out into nothing or meaninglessness, “Starling” adds meaning through a steady bassline that anchors the swells and melodies drifting above it. Creating haunting, otherworldly textures (in reverse) :: “All a blur” is where Deschamps uses backward recordings and noises for reversed melodies. Writing reversed melodies is a craft that’s both detailed and tricky. When you reverse a recording, the attack and decay of each note flip—what was a sharp pluck becomes a slow swell, and what was a fade becomes an abrupt cut. This means that composing in reverse requires you to think backward about how sounds will evolve. It’s not just playing something and hitting reverse; it’s imagining how the reversed version will sound and then recording the forward version in a way that creates the desired effect when flipped. Sometimes it works beautifully, creating haunting, otherworldly textures. Sometimes it doesn’t, the timing feels off, the melody doesn’t resolve the way you’d hoped, or the reversed artifacts distract from the composition. Deschamps fits this perfectly here. At its core, “all a blur” sounds nightmarish, but it really isn’t. The reversed elements create an unsettling undercurrent, but the piece never collapses into darkness. It’s tense without being oppressive. Air Signs rests at its distinct sound. Everything is pieced together very well, and all the noises, melodies, and synths are family—they all align track after track. Deschamps has a gift for cohesion. Even when he’s working with degraded loops, reversed recordings, and heavily processed guitar, nothing feels fragmented. Everything belongs. The mastering by Peter Andersson helps too, giving the release a warm, unified sheen that ties the six tracks together. Air Signs is limited to 100 copies on factory-pressed CD, packaged in a unique discbox slider case with a soft-touch finish. For fans of guitar-based ambient and electroacoustic music, this is a strong addition to both Deschamps‘ catalog and Dronarivm‘s growing discography. Air Signs is available on Dronarivm. [Bandcamp] Air Signs by anthéne

Her latest single “Mustard Seed” pairs her with Tikur Anbessa Records, the Los Angeles label run by Fikir Amlak, a singer, multi-instrumentalist and producer with 20 years in the business, and London’s King Alpha, a Ghanaian-born, West London producer and sound system operator who has spent years pressing dub and roots riddims to vinyl and taking them to sound system stages across Europe and beyond. Amlak and King Alpha have worked together since 2014, giving the record a production backbone with a decade of roots credibility behind it. The track rides a heavy steppas riddim, deep bassline and crisp percussion giving her warm, focused delivery the room to push the message forward. In both biblical and Rastafari tradition the mustard seed is faith that grows from almost nothing, and for an artist who found Rastafari as a reckoning with Black identity and cultural pride, that image runs through everything she makes, placing her in the line of Marcia Griffiths and Jah9. Stream “Mustard Seed” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Kazayah – Mustard Seed appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.excerpt: Review by andrea — " Pangea e le tre lune" is the fourth album by Il Cerchio d'Oro and was released in 2023 on the independent Black Widow Records label with a line up featuring Franco Piccolini (keyboards), Giuseppe Terribile (bass, vocals), Gino Terribile (drums, percussion, vocals), Piuccio Pradal (guitar, vocals) and Massimo Spica (guitar) plus some prestigious guests such as Donald Lax (violin, from historic Italianprog band Quella Vecchia Locanda), Tolo Marton (guitar, former member
items.body: Review by andrea — " Pangea e le tre lune" is the fourth album by Il Cerchio d'Oro and was released in 2023 on the independent Black Widow Records label with a line up featuring Franco Piccolini (keyboards), Giuseppe Terribile (bass, vocals), Gino Terribile (drums, percussion, vocals), Piuccio Pradal (guitar, vocals) and Massimo Spica (guitar) plus some prestigious guests such as Donald Lax (violin, from historic Italianprog band Quella Vecchia Locanda), Tolo Marton (guitar, former member of Le Orme), Ricky Belloni (guitar, from Nuova Idea and New Trolls), Valerio Piccioli (guitar) and Carlo Deprati (narrative vocals) who contributed to enrich the sound. This album confirms all the good qualities of the band's previous works, with a sound deeply rooted in the seventies yet never overly nostalgic and a music always in service of the storyline. It's a concept alnum that tells of the birth of the Earth with fantasy and fairytale nuances. The lyrics are by Giuseppe Paolino, an old friend of the band, while the beautiful art cover is by Armando Mancini, a talented painter who's behind some seventies iconic prog album covers like those of Quella Vecchia Locanda...The title of the opener, "Pangea", refers to the supercontinent that existed during the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic eras and began to break apart about 200 million years ago. After a dreamlike introduction with piano and flute in the foreground, the music and lyrics evoke a ball of fire that some god has carelessly hurdled into eternity. The music is dense and rich with shifts in tempo and atmosphere, while the lyrics, with nuanced tones, outline the mystery of creation. No one knows exactly how it happened, there are no witnesses, but the flame slowly turned into Earth. So, it's just a strange trick of fate that gave life, almost with childlike innocence, to this new entity that will become a continent and be called Pangea...In "Alla deriva" (Adrift) the music and lyrics describe the new continent floating on dark, restless waters, a lifeless land slowly drifting aimlessly across a frightening landscape. Three amused moons watch over it from the sky...Introduced by a dreamlike section with the violin in the forefront, "Dialogo" (Dialogue) evokes the image of a shooting star causing the fragmentation of the new continent. The fractured land turns to the wind and the moon, giving rise to an imaginary dialogue. The wind pushes Pangea onto the sea waves and lifts it to seek a new path, while a friendly moon watches from above and smiles, accompanying it into the darkness of the night..."Le tre lune" (The three moons) is a complex piece, rich in nuances and changes in rhythm and atmosphere. The music and lyrics evoke the image of three moons slowly revolving around the Earth. The first is red, the second yellow, and the third is black, blending into the darkness of the night. Each moon chases the other, casting colourful reflections on the sea of ​​Pangea. These marvellous reflections spark a dispute between the three vain moons. Eventually, the yellow and red moons implode and dissolve, leaving only the black moon in the sky of Pangea. Over time, the black moon learns to wear yellow and red colurs, while it tires of black and, from then on, wears it, albeit elegantly, only occasionally...The instrumental introduction to "Dal nulla cos�" (Out of nowhere, like that) might recall Le Orme, but the piece then develops in an original way. The music and lyrics describe a desolate and hostile landscape: a dark sea, brown earth, earthquakes and storms, winds and active volcanoes. Who would have thought that life could arise in such a place? Yet there was no past nor fear, and life began its journey toward an unknown future,...The next piece, "E la vita inizi�" (And life began), dreamily describes the beginning of life on Earth. Beneath a carpet of stars, Pangea continued its journey unstoppably, driven by a rebellious sea. The continent broke apart, then reunited, changing shape several times until reaching its current form. Chance, chemistry, and the sun's rays helped life emerge from the seabed, now less dark and threatening. An evolutionary process destined to never stop...The album's final piece, "Crisi" (Crises), is listed as a bonus track and has nothing to do with the concept. It's a hard rock song (with obvious references to Deep Purple) released as a single in 1981 and occasionally played by the band during their concerts. It deals with the economic crisis and social values ​​of the late 1970s...On the whole, an excellent work that should find a place in your Italianprog collection!

items.body: Review by sgtpepper — It's great that the band release a live album in this line-up incarnation. Essential pieces of the 73-74 era are included, one from the masterful debut album and even a packed jam "Asbury Park".There are many instrumental highlights but the interplay between the bass and drums is worth calling out. Bruford clearly enjoys a room for improvisation and Wetton's aggressive playing style complements the essential dynamic sound.I have the newer USA live version, which includes "Fractures" which I'm very happy to be included. The density, tension and guitar playing are magnificent, especially in the ominous end.To sum it up, the material and playing are excellent but one would hope for a better overall sound (even though the instruments are distinctive) and greater length ;)

items.body: Review by FalconBleck — #59 ReviewI found this one because of a certain vocalist from another prog rock band that I love, any recentsurprise is welcome, I'm sure that I haven't heard everything in the Genesis world, is just that Istruggle finding new things to hear, and this was and is what I needed.- Watcher Of The Skies (Hush): Already an interesting proposal with a different sound, then adifferent introduction that starts with the chords, and then the main riff in acoustic guitar soundsgreat, then in familiar territory, but still very modern, it works really good for a new version ofthe song, no complaints, I'm sure that I come back to this version from time to time, well doneHush.- Firth Of Fifth (Over The Garden Wall): Very similar to the original, barely any difference, doneas faithful as it can be, as much as I like how it sounds, I sometimes feel like I would ratherlisten to the original, since they are so similar, but at the same time, they are so similar thatthis version can satisfy me from listening to the original. There are subtle differences, thekeyboard middle part is done with an acoustic guitar, at least the main part, then it goes back tokeyboard, it sounds great, but again, so similar, honestly well done, the quality on this album hasbeen great so far. Ok, people want to know about the guitar solo, some people only seem to careabout that, I get it, its great, but there's more song to be enjoyed, anyways, the solo is like amix between Steve and Daryl, that's also great, a very well done Firth Of Fifth.- Undertow (Jay Tausig): Continuing with quality and versions being very similar, this one is reallyclose again, however, this one sounds a bit more melancholic, the voice has less power than Phil,its like closer to Tony Banks, and he made the song, add to this the faded keyboards, and you have aversion that feels more melancholic. The piano sound is also more up-front, I keep coming back tothis version for those slight differences.- Ripples (Annie Haslam): I found this album through this song, the vocalist of Renaissance playinga Genesis song? I have to listen to this, and then I found that it was Ripples, least to say myexpectations were very high. Then I heard it, and at first it was everything I expected, she doesher own spin into the song and sounds great, however, no solo, instead a more happy version of thesong, that I kind of dig, but at the same time, I would like to hear Annie singing over the originalinstrumental done by Genesis, at least this is the closest we can get.- Back in NYC (Kevin Gilbert): Kind of prophetic in a way, Genesis did a lighter version of TheLamb, and this one starts like that, then it obviously goes back to being the usual song, there wasmaybe a need for this to be 2 versions, but it doesn't matter, the song introduces some new ideas,the quiet parts are more quiet, and sometimes even funky, it really plays more with thejuxtaposition of moods that the original song introduces, and while I like the vocals and what's inhere, I still want to listen to the original more, and the ending with the NYC atmosphere issomething I truly don't like, just stop the song beforethat comes.- For Absent Friends (Richard Sinclair): I really admire this version of the song, the vocals areendearing, the instrumentation feels richer with the added strings and harpsichord, and if thatwasn't enough, the song gets extended to almost twice its length, this is definitely a must listenfrom this album. - Mama (Magellan): I like how the drum pattern sounds, most of it gets respected, however, I'm notsure about the rest of the sounds, for a moment the song is just fine, the introduction is fast,which is nice, but then the first laugh gets ruined by an uninspired drum roll, the voice justdoesn't get there, for some reason the notes are all high as soon as possible, it just doesn't work,its as if they wanted to be louder than the original just for the sake of it. Finally we reach thelaugh, and again, its too much, the point of the song is that it was simple and tense, if you wantedto add more into the song, it would've been a good idea to hear the pre-release version, however, itwasn't released back then yet. I will just say, for a moment it was very promising, production isgood, I have no doubt that these are good musicians, just obviously not Genesis.- Man Of Our Times (Enchant): I usually don't mention production, because my copy of the CD could bethe problem, well, I'm listening from YT, and this one sounds weak for some reason, like its lackingsomething, but that's probably the upload, ignoring all that, this version is very comparable to theoriginal, except for everything that sounds a bit weaker, the strongs are the over-drive guitar andthe background voices that sound louder than in the original, that also do a more noticeablefun stereo play, which is a production win. Honestly, this version is fine, but I would ratherlisten to the original, there's nothing that makes me comeback to this version because its sosimilar, the over-drive doesn't convince me.- Many Too Many (Peter Bardens): One advantage this version has over the original is that the firstincrease is more subtle, and the second is bigger, while in the original both feel similar, however,the original has a very cool guitar solo that's heavily reduced in this version, that could've beena very neat improvement.- Entangled (Shadow Gallery): Incredibly similar to the original, well done instrumental, the voiceson the chorus though sound like the three musketeers, it doesn't work and it takes me away from thesong. The guitars sound very clean and pleasant, the ending is not as strong, yet very close,overall a good version that feels new, it just needs to fix the chorus. Minus points for the fade-out instead of having an ending.- Squonk (Cairopaiva): There are some decisions I don't like, the instruments seem to alternatebetween ideas that don't work well, they add things that could be welcome, but they aren't cleverenough, they feel out of place, the guitar at the start, the drums a bit after that, the best thingabout this song is the voice, the vocalist does a very good job, sounds fresh and respectful, hefits the song well enough, which is surprising by how difficult it is. The ending is ruined here,why do you have talking, and a very early fade-out? Terrible decision.- I Know What I Like (Crack The Sky): What is this? Crack The Sky? They are great, but what was theidea here? Being different just for the sake of it? It doesn't fit the rest of this album as well,its so weird, but I kind of dig the style change, it sounds more scary than happy, I think that'ssomething good, but other than that, this is just a curiosity, they managed something veryinteresting here, it doesn't sound like anything on this album, or Crack The Sky, or any decisionthat Genesis would've taken with this song, but it still sounds a bit like Genesis, its so weird.- The Carpet Crawlers (Michael Zentner): I'm sorry, the voice doesn't do it for me, its too forced,the kind of forced voice you get away with in high school, like no one told you that it wasn't good.This is sadly one of worst Carpet Crawlers I have heard so far, I'm sorry for being so harsh, Ireally don't like it, the drums are too loud an static, the strings are barely here and I completelymiss the keyboard I love so much, the guitar is fine, but not enough... This is definitely a CarpetCrawlers, but its just so under-cooked, and the single voice is over-done, totally missing the pointof the song. The best I can say that it seems to be a respectful attempt, although the forced voicefeels like a mockery at times, I just can't recommend this one.- Keep It Dark (World Trade): Now this one is weaker, but it respects even the smallest details atthe best it can, however, it really lacks an stronger bass and keyboards, the voice is fine,obviously not Phil, but its well done. The differences are so small that they barely matter, andalso the song ends faster, well done but not enough.In conclusion, this album is a bit of a mix bag, there are some interesting proposals and even someideas that can be good to listen as a new version that compliments the original, however, I don'tthink that any of these versions represent the best of what this artists can do, I appreciate theeffort a lot and the amount of Genesis eras that they covered, I'm glad that this exists, I justwish that it was better and that it had a better name, because some of what's in here needs to beheard by Genesis and prog rock fans.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — Wow, what a hidden gem! Capitolo 6 was one of the countless Italian bands from this period who flirted with progressive rock, but for me, I'd say they're one of the finest examples of a Rock Progressivo Italiano band that just never got its footing while active and never got the praise it deserves years later. The one album they did make, Frutti Per Kagua, is an amazing compilation of engaging jams, technical progressive rock, and twinges of jazz rock, all mixed in with a heavy edge that echoes what the band's English counterparts were doing at the same time. I noticed a very clear similarity to Jumbo, not only musically but vocally as well. Their singer, Riccardo Bartolotti (who also does some guitar and flute here and there), has that same raspy and intense quality that catches your ear whenever you listen to Alvaro Fella sing on a Jumbo album. On the topic of the personnel, Jimmy Santerini plays keyboards and does some singing parts, Lorenzo Donati does the drumming and is also listed as helping with the vocals, Maurizio Romani plays the bass, and Loriano Berti performs as the band's saxophonist and flutist. The record opens with the phenomenal twenty-minute-long title track, which is my favorite piece on the whole record and contains some extremely interesting and well-put-together music. It's a fascinating mix of bluesy, guitar-heavy rock music, blissful folk compositions, emotionally driving melodies and jamming and is overall a great experience that has a great sense of direction and identity. It really goes to show how far this group could've gone if they had gotten the recognition they deserved. Side two has the other three tracks, none of which are quite as long but generally have a good frame for length. The energy on side one continues as each piece is full of captivating moments of pure power and very dynamic material that truly breathes and flows greatly. The fast-paced, almost jazz fusion-like rhythms are only contrasted by the calming seas of acoustic material, but overall the music here is very much on the electric side of things. Overall, it's all very strong and a great representation of Rock Progressivo Italiano at its core, with both charming and grittier tones of the scene. In conclusion, I would highly recommend this band for anyone wanting to expand their knowledge on the map of Italian prog. It's very reminiscent of some of the classics while also feeling fresh and fun. It may not be an absolute essential, but to me it is deserving of a very strong 4.25/5.

items.body: Justin Taylor’s Clavecin XX presents an intriguing selection of solo and ensemble works by Bartók, Françaix, Górecki, Poulenc, and Manuel de Falla, placing a traditionally antiquated instrument squarely in a modern context. For this recording, Taylor utilizes a 1970s harpsichord by Anthony Sidey that hybridizes elements from 1920s Pleyels with much earlier models. This versatility, the artist notes, allowed him to rely on a single instrument throughout the diverse recital. Indeed, the Sidey instrument’s profile encompasses an array of personalities and sonorities that are brilliantly unveiled across the album. Clavecin XX Amazon Presto Apple Referencing Baroque forms like the Toccata and Minuet, Jean Françaix’s Concerto features a distinctive tonal language that places the harpsichord in a curious perspective. Deriving its energy from Taylor’s full-bodied tremolos, Toccata I is further animated by piquant string pizzicatos that add a sprightly, balletic quality. Sharing a similar texture but adopting a diametrically opposed, lyrical profile, Toccata II allows the keyboardist to trace horizontal lines with a pleasing legato, its fluidity highlighting refreshing harmonic progressions. Demonstrating the chameleon-like quality of the instrument, Taylor shines in the Minuet. Here, the harpsichord occasionally resembles a dulcimer or a Japanese koto, bringing a fitting dimension to a multifaceted compositional language steeped in Impressionism, cinema, and dance. Serving as a stark departure from the preceding charm, the selection by Henryk Górecki is deeply stimulating in how its two movements employ repetitional minimalism to cast the harpsichord in strikingly different lights. Taylor’s even-keeled perpetuum mobile in the Allegro molto is insistent, clashing unapologetically with the equally stubborn, static ensemble part. The resulting sonority is mechanical, bordering on the computerized. Driven by relentless chords, the subsequent Vivace marcatissimo builds profound tension. The performers do a remarkable job maintaining metronomic precision, molding a conflict that eventually comes to a head as spectacular harmonic collisions evolve into a frenetic sonic assault—an effect most certainly intended given the music’s inherent angst. While Manuel de Falla’s selection injects rhythmic vitality into the program, Francis Poulenc‘s Concert champêtre stands out for its high-spirited, imaginative execution. Written for Wanda Landowska (an artist Taylor cites as a major inspiration), the concerto operates in a Neo-Baroque style. Conjuring stately authority in their slow introduction, the orchestra sets the stage for the keyboardist to bring elegant liveliness to the Allegro section. The Finale is arguably the most engaging movement due to its sheer eclecticism. Launching as a virtuosic Gigue, it quickly diversifies to encompass hints of improvisation, a march, and elements drawn from Romantic and Neo-Romantic symphonies. Adapting to this complex structure admirably, the performers ensure no particular reference feels contrived or out of place. In this work, as in the other concertos, the Orchestre National de Lille under Chloé Dufresne is an attentive partner, articulating the clever counterpoint clearly while never overshadowing the harpsichord. Justin Taylor. Photo © Jean-Baptiste Millot. Turning to the solo works, the opening selection from Bartók‘s Mikrokosmos serves as a brief but wonderfully rendered introduction, establishing the character of the entire program through its interplay between consonance and dissonance. Taylor’s precise articulation gives the notes ample space to resonate, allowing listeners to appreciate them individually while sympathetic resonances beautifully mingle. Paying homage to György Ligeti’s landmark harpsichord work Continuum (which famously transforms the instrument into an ominous, persistent buzz), Stéphane Gassot’s Bluesinuum offers a gentler take. Although it references a similar trill-like texture in its middle section, Gassot’s approach is notably more subdued. Taylor’s bluesy rhythms possess both snap and fluidity, while occasional lower-register rumbles introduce a welcome playfulness to the mix. Concluding the album is a familiar tune: Scott Joplin’s Maple Leaf Rag. While the execution is solid and the artist’s transcription remains faithful to the original, hearing this piece on a harpsichord proves difficult to digest. The timbre of the instrument simply does not suit the repertoire, transforming the music’s inherent jauntiness into something rather heavy and labored. Perhaps this iconic rag is best left to its intended medium, the piano. Taylor’s interview in the liner notes portrays him as a well-spoken, meticulous musician who has invested significant research into his repertoire prior to performance. With the exception of the final track, this curation stands as an engaging testament to the harpsichord’s vast capabilities well beyond its traditional Baroque boundaries. Though not all the pieces make for easy listening, Taylor undeniably maximizes the instrument’s technical and musical capacity. items.body: The Portland, Oregon-based synth-punk duo Point Line Plane has released its self-titled debut album, “Point Line Plane,” on SKiN GRAFT Records. The release marks the first-ever vinyl pressing of the record, which was originally co-released on CD by Xeroid Records and Sincere Brutality in 2003 and has been out of print for more than twenty years. Formats include LP, CD, digital and an Ultimate Edition. The vinyl edition is pressed on 8-Bit Blue Vinyl, limited to 1500 numbered copies worldwide. Packaging includes a double-sided “Footlong” OBI with artwork by Portland designer E*Rock. A CD edition includes one bonus track not available on the LP. The Ultimate Edition adds a large-format booklet containing a memoir titled “The Future Belongs to Analog Loyalists” by guitarist Mitsuru Tabata, a comic by Rob Syers, and a pull-out poster. Point Line Plane by Point Line Plane The album was recorded and engineered by Steve Albini and Zeni Geva. Mastering of the original release was handled by Denis Blackham and Martin Bowes. Vinyl mastering for this 2026 pressing was completed in December 2025 by Carl Saff and Bob Weston. The lead single is “Death Dance 2000”, which has an official music video. About Point Line Plane Point Line Plane was formed in Portland, Oregon, around 2002 by vocalist and keyboardist Joshua Blanchard and drummer Nathan Carson as a synth-and-drums duo. Blanchard had previously performed as part of the Sensualists. Carson co-founded the Portland doom metal band Witch Mountain in 1997 and has run the booking agency Nanotear. The band’s self-titled debut was recorded and released in 2003, co-issued on CD by Xeroid Records and Sincere Brutality. That year the duo also released the single “Curse Chorus Curse / Sh…Boom” on S-S Records, contributed a cover of “Give The Future A Break” to a Screamers tribute compilation, and completed a split release with The Planet. In late 2003, Howard Gillam (also known as Supersprite) joined on second synth, expanding the lineup to a trio. As a trio, the band recorded “Smoke Signals,” released in 2004 on SKiN GRAFT Records. The band also produced the score for the feature documentary “Haunters.” Point Line Plane disbanded in 2005 after approximately 150 live performances. Both founding members continued other work. Blanchard also performs as Major Hex. Carson remained active with Witch Mountain, which has toured internationally and released records on Profound Lore Records and Svart Records. He also hosts The Heavy Metal Sewïng Cïrcle on XRAY FM, runs Nanotear Booking, and has published fiction. The original duo, Blanchard and Carson, announced their return in 2026 when SKiN GRAFT Records proposed the remastered vinyl reissue of the debut. “Point Line Plane” (SKiN GRAFT Records) is out now.

items.body: Russian punk collective Pussy Riot announced “CYKA,” their debut full-length album, scheduled for release on June 12, 2026, on digital streaming platforms. The fourteen-track record compresses fourteen years of the group’s activity – including protest actions, imprisonment and exile – into a single body of work. The album title translates from Russian as “bitch.” Lead single “Candy Dopamine,” featuring Avenged Sevenfold, is out now with an official music video on YouTube. “Candy Dopamine” was co-written by Pussy Riot with Avenged Sevenfold vocalist M. Shadows and guitarist Zacky Vengeance. The track mixes pop with alternative rock and features guest vocals from M. Shadows alongside heavy guitar work. Pussy Riot founder Nadya Tolokonnikova described the song as a statement on prescription and designer drug culture: “It started with my dependence on antidepressants, but it’s also looking at everyone now, mentalhealthmaxxing and looksmaxxing via pills and injections. It’s not a judgment, it’s just an observation, and my personal experience with these things is that I have to be in a long-term relationship with them for my PTSD and depression.” This is the second collaboration between Avenged Sevenfold and Pussy Riot. In 2023, Tolokonnikova appeared on a reworked version of the Avenged Sevenfold track “We Love You,” re-released as “We Love You Moar,” raising awareness of the situation of LGBTQ+ people in Russia. The album’s earlier single “Disobey” was released in May 2026. Its music video consists of footage from Pussy Riot’s “Storm of Venice” protest action at the 61st Venice Biennale, in which more than fifty members of the collective stormed the Russian pavilion with clouds of pink smoke. Ukrainian activist group FEMEN joined the demonstration, which was staged in protest at Russia’s return to the international art event. The 90-second track features distorted guitars, shouted vocals and chants of “disobey,” with lyrics in English and Russian condemning fascism and political silence. ‘CYKA’: collaborators, tracklist, and Putin challenge Other confirmed contributors on “CYKA” include B-Real of Cypress Hill (on the track “Gore”) and singer-songwriter Salem Ilese (on “Utopia”). Russian President Vladimir Putin is listed as a contributor on the self-titled track “Cyka.” Tolokonnikova adds: “I’m not gonna give him royalties though, they can add it to my list of crimes.” Tolokonnikova also announced a public challenge to Putin to fight her at the UFC Freedom 250 event, scheduled for June 14 at the White House. In her statement, she says: “All these old men ruining the world right now act tough, but we see through their fragile egos, and I’m not afraid to call them out. I challenge President Putin to a cage match. He loses? He gets the fuck out of Ukraine.” About Pussy Riot Pussy Riot is a Russian punk and protest collective founded in Moscow in 2011. The group operates as a loose, rotating collective but is closely associated with founders Nadya Tolokonnikova (also known as Nadya Tolokno) and Maria Alyokhina (known as Masha). The group staged performances in public spaces across Moscow as acts of political protest, often wearing brightly colored balaclavas. In February 2012, three members – Tolokonnikova, Alyokhina and Yekaterina Samutsevich – were arrested following a performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. They were convicted of “hooliganism motivated by religious hatred” and sentenced to two years in a penal colony. Samutsevich was released on appeal in October 2012; Tolokonnikova and Alyokhina served their full sentences, released in December 2013. The trial attracted international attention. Following their release, Tolokonnikova and Alyokhina continued their political activism and released music under the Pussy Riot name. The group collaborated with Boys Noize on “Rage” in 2021, and with Boyfriend on the electropop single “Dance With the Devil” in 2023. In July 2025, a new Russian law criminalized searching for Pussy Riot content online. In April 2026, Tolokonnikova was formally indicted by Russia’s Investigative Committee for alleged violations of the country’s “foreign agent” law. “CYKA” is Pussy Riot’s debut full-length album. It is released June 12, 2026.

items.body: Following the previous album “Select”, which mainly featured a curated selection of tracks taken from Subverge’s existing releases, this new opus brings together a collection of unreleased, previously unknown, remix, and collaborative tracks. Henrik Karlsson personally selected the thirteen songs included here. There is perhaps slightly more diversity in terms of sound and influences on this record compared to Select, although the foundation of the compositions remains very much intact. Subverge continues to craft a highly distinctive form of Dark Ambient, occasionally enriched with slow rhythms and subtle percussion. Throughout the album, one can clearly hear Karlsson’s unmistakable fascination with Electro music and his irresistible urge for experimentation and sonic exploration. The result is a deeply cinematic work that, aside from a few vocal contributions, remains largely instrumental. Subverge excels at building dark atmospheres and allowing them to evolve gradually, much like the tension unfolding within a thriller film. Among the collaborations, the outstanding track with Access To Arasaka deserves special mention, serving as a true apotheosis of the album. Above all, Henrik Karlsson once again confirms his extraordinary talent for composing visionary and dark Ambient music, distinguished by intelligent sound design and remarkably refined production work. (Rating:8). Listen to “Purple Storm”: https://aliensproduction.bandcamp.com/track/purple-storm

items.body: The Witch Said No is a relatively obscure project from Russia that has been active for several years and has already released a number of recordings in its home country, including a debut album. Very little is known about the project itself, which only adds to its mysterious aura. Earlier this year, the band released a new EP through the Slovak label Aliens Production, featuring three new tracks alongside six remixes. The Witch Said No delivers a powerful form of Dark-Electro driven by bombastic heavy beats and overwhelming repetitive sequences, topped with an almost completely unintelligible, hateful vocal style. The title track is certainly an interesting discovery, while the two remaining new songs follow a similar direction but prove slightly less convincing. The remixes of the title track were created by KIFOTH, Deadjump, Human Vault, Novakill, and TC75. The EP also includes an alternative version of an older track. What stands out most here is undoubtedly the title track itself, which shows strong potential, alongside several successful remixes — especially Novakill’s contribution, which turns out to be my personal favorite. (Rating:7). Listen to “Call The Dead”: https://aliensproduction.bandcamp.com/track/call-the-dead

items.body: With the cards you hold But who’s on trial Carve their names Declare your crimes Since we last checked in, Brooklyn-bred noise rock quartet Clone have been hard at work, honing their craft on stage and in the studio. The band has just returned from a short stint on the road and offer up a blistering video for single “Care to Try?” from their EP of the same name, which was released in October of last year. “Care to Try?” follows up the band’s debut album CL.1, released in 2024. “Care to Try?” is a powerful anthem of resistance, targeting and taunting the current political administration in the USA with biting lyrics and hard-hitting, guitar-driven discord. Opening with short burst of feedback and a catchy, yet incisive melody, the track quickly takes hold and goes straight for the jugular, with vocalist LG Galleon seething and shouting lyrics of rebellion above the din to dizzying effect. Shades of bands such as Live Skull, Naked Raygun, The Chameleons, and Killing Joke can be heard throughout the track, which eventually explodes into a cacophonous, scorched-earth coda that commands reflection and action. Filmed and colored by Devan Davies and edited by Galleon, the video for “Care to Try?” perfectly reflects the song’s fiery intent. “With their second go-around things just seem even more hopeless than before,” adds Galleon, “and this video tries to capture he frustration of an ever increasing world gone mad.” Check out the track and video below, and be sure to catch the band live this Thursday at Berlin Under A in NYC. items.body: When the fields of the cross were burning Our paths would go their separate ways Somehow we were always learning Learning from our own mistakes DETOXi’s In Laughter carries the strange charge of unfinished business: a song born in the pandemic years, finally given its full second life. Southern California deathrock has always known how to turn damage into drama, but this track carries itself with a bruised grandeur that feels earned, shaped by absence, distance, and the weird ache of art left suspended when the world stopped mid-sentence. Musically, the song feels cut from a generous, high-hearted lineage. There is the romantic sweep of The Cult, the broad reach of Midnight Oil, the open-road lift of Big Country, the hard tension of Killing Joke, and a flash of Aztec Camera’s bittersweet clarity in the way melody and feeling are allowed to meet head-on. Jennings sings straight into a memory with a killer anthemic chorus, while the band pushes forward with a handsome urgency, turning grief into motion and ultimately release. Lyrically, In Laughter traces a relationship marked by fear, separation, and unresolved longing, returning again and again to the idea that love survives through joy rather than pain. Burning fields, graves, frozen time, and repeated invitations give the song the feeling of a letter written after the worst has already happened, when tenderness becomes the last brave act left. Director Braedon Roller treats the performance video like a transmission from a band interrupted by history, then summoned back by the force of unfinished feeling. “For this project, I wanted to borrow stylistically from David Lynch’s Blue Velvet,” says Roller. “I’ve always been struck by the candy-colored clown scene and thought that lighting and mood would be perfect inspiration for a music video. I also pulled from films like [Robert Eggers’] The VVitch and…Nosferatu: dark, desaturated imagery living in blue and orange tones. The song has this haunting beauty to it, and I wanted to capture that while really focusing on the emotion of the performance. One technique I like to use is having the singer perform in double time while overcranking the camera, then slowing the footage down in post so the performance lands perfectly on tempo. It creates this strange, hypnotic effect that felt right for this song. The video was filmed across two separate nights, over 4 years, and the edit was incredibly labor-intensive, but I’m really proud of how it turned out.” Watch the video for In Laughter below: The backstory of the band has the cruel timing of a rock-and-roll fable. DETOXi played the vinyl release show for their debut album, First Flesh, on Leap Year Day in 2020, only days before record stores and venues closed, putting the band’s momentum into a deep freeze. During the uncertainty that followed, they kept recording, releasing the In Laughter EP in March 2021 and beginning work on a video for the title track. Then life scattered the pieces: Derek Jennings relocated to Portland, Oscar Estrada and John Crerar started HEAD CUT, and Matt Barks turned his focus toward projects outside music. DETOXi Still, In Laughter kept moving. DJs found it. Fans passed it around. Social media did its strange little underground magic trick, carrying the song into new circles while longtime listeners kept asking when DETOXi might return to the stage. Listen to In Laughter below and order the EP here. In Laughter EP by DETOXI And DETOXi return to the stage Friday, June 26, for their first show since the pandemic, celebrating Crerar’s 50th birthday at Vaquero y Mar in Ventura, California…the same venue where they last played before lockdown. The lineup brings together their earlier incarnation Maask, HEAD CUT, Guilty Strangers, and Dusk At Midnight. For DETOXi, the circle closes with feedback, friendship, and laughter carrying through the wreckage. Get tickets to the show here. items.body: This is my house I’m pretty sure Or did I turn the wrong way at the corner store? There are few things more quietly terrifying than realizing a place meant to hold us no longer seems to know us. A home can turn uncanny without changing shape: the same walls, the same rooms, the same door, and yet the air feels wrong. A party can become alien in an instant. A familiar street can suddenly feel like a wrong turn. Sometimes the most frightening estrangement is not from other people, but from our own certainty — that small internal rupture when memory, perception, and instinct stop agreeing with one another. That uneasy threshold is where Berlin-based quartet Agatha is Dead! place their new single “Strangers.” Taken from their forthcoming debut album Concrete, due out on September 11, the track is a study in dissociation, displacement, and the peculiar horror of feeling locked out of a life that should belong to you. “Strangers” opens with a danceable drum beat and a thick, softly carried shadow-laced bass groove, quickly joined by a rubbery, reverbed guitar figure that glints like a melody half-remembered. It almost masquerades as a piano hook: bright, repetitive, and singable, but with enough coldness in its edges to keep the mood unsettled. There is a trace of the icy, Eastern European post-punk guitar language popularized by acts like Molchat Doma, but Agatha is Dead! bend that familiar vocabulary into something more elastic, melodic, and contemporary. The result is a sound stripped down to its essentials without feeling nostalgic for its own sake. When the vocals enter, roughly half a minute in, they arrive controlled and rhythmic, carrying a poetic cadence with a sighing edge. Rather than pushing the song into melodrama, the performance tightens the tension: the melody becomes more insistent, the groove more infectious, and the chorus gradually takes on an anthemic charge. By the time the central cry of “strangers in my house” rises into view, the track has turned paranoia into a hook — something intimate, frightening, and strangely cathartic. Lyrically, “Strangers” follows a narrator trying to re-enter what should be their own space, only to find every sign of belonging destabilized. The house is familiar, or at least it should be. The faces are not. The details have shifted. The mind keeps searching for a rational explanation — a wrong turn, a misplaced key, a simple mistake — but the deeper dread is that something has gone wrong in perception itself. The refrain’s fear of being “locked me out” lands less like a literal complaint than a plea to return to the self. At around the 2:45 mark, the song shifts into a slower, eerier passage, letting the anguish breathe before the rhythm gathers itself again for the final stretch. It is here that the track’s sense of domestic unease becomes something larger: a fear of being made foreign in your own body, your own memory, your own home. And for anyone who has experienced tragedy and turmoil in their life, loss of continuity is one of the most unsettling things one can experience. Listen to “Strangers” below: Formed during the long winter of 2021, Agatha is Dead! began as a collaboration between Lilly and Noah, building songs in isolation before bringing them into the open. Drawing from the stark emotional landscape of Joy Division and the nocturnal melancholy of The Cure, the band’s sound merges restraint with intensity — a tension that has become central to their live presence. Joined by Joey Ramone Hansen on drums and Arthur on bass, the group quickly established itself within Berlin’s live circuit. Since signing to Duchess Box Records in 2025, Agatha is Dead! have built a reputation for performances that feel both intimate and unsettling. Following showcase appearances at SXSW, the band returned to Berlin for a sold-out headline show at Lido, confirming a growing presence beyond the city’s underground. With Concrete on the horizon, they now move into a wider run of German and European dates, including Reeperbahn Festival and their largest headline show to date at SO36 in Berlin on 25 February 2027. With “Strangers,” Agatha is Dead! step further into a world of dislocation and unease, where the familiar no longer offers comfort and what we once knew begins to blur. Agatha is Dead! items.body: Damage Code Digital Slaves Miseria Records Damage Code is the new project from Carlos Grabstein and Ben Bunzen of 89s✝︎ and Hammershøi respectively, and deals in a very specific style of old school EBM. Forgoing the oft-taken route of Nitzer Ebb and DAF worship, the duo instead deal in a sound that recalls a swathe of body music acts from Europe that emerged in the early 90s (think Escalator and Aircrash Bureau) that took advantage of advancements in digital electronics while maintaining a healthy amount of grit in their design. As such, Digital Slaves is a record that doesn’t break much in the way of new ground, but makes an impact by keeping its tracks impactful and fast moving, usually running a single groove as hard as possible from beginning to end. Grabstein and Bunzen certainly know what they’re doing with that approach and it pays off well in plenty of the record’s nine tracks; “I’m Sick of These Pigs” has a rhythm that just keeps getting heavier as it progresses, the gravitational pull of its bassline and drums warping its sweeping noise, and monotone vocals towards it. Alternately, Notausgang collab “Monotonia” is all about how its gated pads and samples and echoing synthlines create syncopation, the bass tuned down to a low rattle. There’s a real charm to just how rough and ready Damage Code keep matters without repeating themselves too often. There’s a healthy dose of funk in the awkward tripping-over-its-own-feet synthline on “Menschen im Glitch” and the chintzy fm stabs of “Esclavo Digital”, but neither track cannibalizes the other’s appeal through repetition. A lot of it has to do with pretty canny if uncomplicated sound design choices, such as the wonky spring reverb and belt sander saturation of “Lessons in Pain” and the claustrophobic delays of “Berlin”, which sounds like it’s closing in on you if listened to on headphones. Old school body music is almost a genre that lives and dies by how it balances the appeal of its throwback approach without just recreating the same songs over and over again. It’s weird to think of such a straightforward genre having much in the way of subtlety, but on Digital Slaves Damage Code certainly make a case for how much you can squeeze out of it through strength of craft. Buy it. Digital Slave by DAMAGE CODE The post Damage Code, “Digital Slaves” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
