items.body:
Rightfully described as a thinking (wo)man's jazz musician, trumpeter-composer-bandleader Steven Bernstein makes deeply cerebral music no matter whether with his own ensembles such as Sexmob and Millennial Territory Orchestra or in heady collaborations with other artists such Jacob Fred Jazz Odyssey (see Race Riot Suite (Royal Potato Family, 2011)).

In fact, the products of his imagination resound with such visceral force that those creations render an impact comparable to his membership in Levon Helm's Midnight Ramble Band (or MTO's tribute to Sly Stone). ResoNation Trio and Ultra Resonance, are similarly charged, the former a forward-thinking yet traditionalist-leaning project for which Bernstein recruited the estimable rhythm section of bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, the latter is a reimagining of that threesome's music overseen by pedigreed engineer and producer Scotty Hard (a long-time collaborator of visionaries unto themselves, Medeski Martin & Wood).

The former is as skeletal as the latter is dense. Yet the two recordings, distinctly different in concept and execution, are nevertheless inextricably linked. Each, in its own way, is a thought-provoking piece, with the respective virtues redolent when played separately or together in sequence, either in the configuration of the single CD or the double vinyl package.

The abstract likes of Bernstein-Colley-Waits' "Turf" benefit as much from the space in the arrangement as the linear progression the three pursue in "Pettiford." Meanwhile, corresponding titles of the companion piece, such as "Rubidium," function similarly, gateways into more or less otherworldly realms (though perhaps not as mesmerizing as the source of that concept, dub reggae recordings by Burning Spear on Garvey's Ghost (Island Records, 1976)).

It is not necessary to listen to Ultra Resonance on headphones to appreciate its aura. Still, that method can reveal more of the multiple layers in the recordings. And, in its own way, that method also proves to be comparatively applicable to the acoustic music: the patient and probing human three-way human interactions that comprise "Woodstock," for instance, radiate both the physical and mental effort involved in the musicianship.

Hard's deeply insistent reformulation of the music through the use of keyboards, various other instruments and percussion, in combination with Jeremy Gustin's varied rhythm devices, emits a presence as haunting as that in the spacious interplay of the ResoNation Trio. Selections from the latter like the one non-original, the blues of "Sitting On Top of the World," resound with comparable levels of mental acumen infused with technical expertise.

A comparatively spooky atmosphere thus pervades most of this seventy-six minutes, even as it is presented in cuts of mostly 3 to 5 minute duration. With its infectious lively cheer, the penultimate track by the trumpeter, bassist and drummer, titled "South," may be the exception to the rule. And the product of Scotty Hard's efforts, such as "Vibranium," are like nothing so much as an individual's inner monologue, filtered through devices, as are so many of our contemporary dialogues.  On the other hand, the acoustic portion effectively constitutes a friendly but lively debate between equals.

Accordingly, the sounds from the three-man ensemble flicker in and out of the well-defined, but dark audio mix during "Argon." And, without ever going on too long to become monotonous, there are just enough similar turns of melody to render more pronounced the heavily rhythmic likes of "Titano." In the end, the overall pacing is that of a well-sequenced live set, without an overabundance of aural esoterica.

It is thus indicative of the seamless yet malleable nature of ResoNation Trio and Ultra Resonance that various elements from each can be interwoven with the other. Reprogramming the CD tracks or alternating the four sides of vinyl extends both the accessibility and the durability of Steven Bernstein and company's eccentric musical orthodoxy.

Turf; Pettiford; Two Shakes; Woodstock; August 3; West; Mammoth; Question; South; Sitting on Top of the World; Argon; Erbium; Chromium; Vibranium; Rubidium; Titano; Radon; Niobium.

Additional Instrumentation

Steven Bernstein: G-trumpet, flugelhorn, EVI; Scotty Hard: Roland 606, Bias BS- 2, Akai MPG 2500, Serato Sampler, Yamaha CS-50, Moog Voyager; lap steel, feedback, percussion. Scott Colley: acoustic bass; Jeremy Gustin: bass drum, floor tom, pandeiro, percussion.

Larry McCray's Heartbreak City, released on Keeping the Blues Alive Records, is steeped in grit, anguish, resilience and hard-won joy. The album reflects the life of a working-class blues man who sharpened his craft in the clubs of Saginaw after shifts on the General Motors assembly line, before touring nationally and eventually across Europe with Albert Collins. Every track carries the emotional weight of decades spent earning success the hard way, drawing deeply from McCray's Arkansas roots while sounding fully grounded in the modern blues tradition.

"Try to Be a Good Man," co-written by McCray, serves as both introduction and mission statement. Riding a chugging roadhouse groove—with a bright, punctuating all-star horn section featuring Dan Fornero, Wayne Bergeron, Andy Martin and Sal Lozano—the song doubles as advice for younger men navigating relationships. McCray's baritone, earthy, warm and unforced, anchors lines such as: "Give her all the love you can and do your best to understand." His guitar work is concise and expressive, delivering sharp, brittle, conversational bends that echo the influence of Little Milton without slipping into imitation. The performance highlights one of McCray's defining strengths: emotional honesty delivered without theatrics.

The title track provides the album's emotional center. Built on a deep blues-rock pocket shaped by the modern production style associated with producers Joe Bonamassa and Josh Smith, "Heartbreak City" unfolds with the restless momentum of an open highway. McCray's stinging guitar lines recall Albert King, while his vocal phrasing again nods to Milton. The song captures the album's defining theme: a man worn down by loss, disappointment and the daily grind, yet still unwilling to surrender. It is weary and determined at the same time, balancing vulnerability with quiet resolve.

On "Everything Falls on Me," McCray channels his frustration through a mid-tempo blues-rock groove shaped by Bo Diddley-style syncopation and terse, declarative guitar figures reminiscent of Chuck Berry. Its lyrics about carrying everyone else's burdens strike a familiar chord without lapsing into self-pity. "When it comes to disaster, Red Cross got nothin' on me / I've cleaned up more messes than the human eye can see / Be it friend or family or someone I just met / They only hit me up for something, anything they can get." McCray sings with a convincing authority that transforms everyday frustrations into something universal.

McCray's songwriting strengths surface again in "Bye Bye Blues," co-written with Charlie Walmsley and nominated for Song of the Year at the 2026 Blues Music Awards. Built around the line, "When I said hello to you, I said goodbye to the blues," the song balances classic blues sentiment with understated optimism and demonstrates McCray's ability to write memorable, emotionally direct material.

Throughout Heartbreak City, McCray honors the artists who shaped him while remaining unmistakably himself. Positioned somewhere between Albert King's fire and Little Milton's silky soulfulness, he delivers performances defined by warmth, grit and emotional clarity. In an era still searching for towering modern blues voices, McCray makes a compelling case for his place near the top of the genre's current generation.

Try To Be A Good Man; Heartbreak City; Bye Bye Blues; Bright Side; Everything Falls On Me; I Know What I Have Done; Keep On Loving My Baby; Hangman; Stop Your Crying; Crazy World.

items.body:
Evidence lives up to its title very well. A lot of music in this fairly short album that makes itself heard with surprising simplicity.

EVIDENCE is a quartet: reeds, trombone, cello and drums. An unusual formation, but one that recalls Henry Threadgill's Zooid from 2015 onwards (without the guitar): In For A Penny, In For A Pound (Pi Recordings, 2015) and Poof. Sol Léna-Schroll (alto saxophone and clarinet) is Threadgill, Jørgen Bjelkerud (trombone) is Jose Davila, Joel Ring that of Christopher Hoffman, and Trym Saugstad Karlsen (drums) is Elliot Humberto Kavee.

The comparison goes no further. For here the music takes flight. The absence of piano and bass is turned to advantage in airy compositions and improvisations, whereas with Threadgill, drums and tuba (which Davila also plays) often take it upon themselves to bring everyone back down to earth. It is a feat of Karlsen's to breathe pulses that propel the music into the air.

Léna-Schroll and Bjelkerud are fellow members of Orchestra for Jazz Composers in Oslo / Orkesteret for Jazzkomponister Oslo (OJKOS) and L'Autre Collectif/Det Andre Kollektivet, a compelling initiative funded by France and Norway since 2019, where the innovative aspects of jazz and sometimes contemporary music are explored, and from which the label Autres Records was born. Bjelkerud and Karlsen appear in Amalie Dahl's Dafnie EXTENDED Live at Moldejazz, Ring in Eon, from Karoline Wallace's quintet, and Karlsen in The Aftermath (Fjordgata Records, 2026), of the major Ingeborg Gravem Sollid quartet, all almost simultaneously released. We are, in other words, at the very top of the tree.

The compositions and arrangements are precise and tightly structured. From them emerge improvisations in which the saxophone and trombone interlock in virtuosic spirals ("Mad Blue"). Freed from any earthly support, improvisation breaks free harmonically from the theme, while maintaining its formal rigour.

The brisk compositions would readily be described as bop in other circumstances, with perhaps a welcome Braxtonian touch. In particular, Léna-Schroll delivers a highly inspired solo in "Infinite Loop." The quieter pieces showcase the timbral contrasts, exemplified by an exquisite dialogue between Ring and Bjelkerud in "Infinite Fase."

This is an album of very high calibre with a great deal of substance. The lively and more measured pieces follow one another in a way that gives the album a fine balance. This beautiful, intelligent album is a breath of fresh air, an invitation to freedom, the opening of morning windows, and a day filled with positive energy.

Mad Blue; Infinite Down (#3); Band Music; Choral; Infinite Loop (#1); Infinite Fase (#2).

items.body:
The fourteen-member Hot House West Swing Orchestra, enabled by Salt Lake City, Utah's nonprofit Hot House West, makes its recorded debut with Joy in Rhythm, Vol. 1, an array of eleven danceable songs, most of which were popular during the Swing Era's golden age in the 1930s and '40s.

This is an album especially designed for dancing; it even includes a booklet that teaches the listener a number of simple dance moves tailored for beginners. In spite of the fact that there are several cursory solos along the way (the longest by violinist Curtis Woodbury), this is not a jazz album per se but one that borrows the rhythms of jazz—most notably swing—to press home its danceable message.

As a guide for dancers, Joy in Rhythm works fairly well. One can imagine a dance floor filled with men and women who are grooving to the music. Remove dancing from the equation, however, and the album reveals a number of flaws, not the least of which is the many liberties taken with the character and tempo of the original compositions—some or even all of which were no doubt deemed necessary to make the finished product more accessible to dancers.

The orchestra's vocalists, Hayley Kirkland and Nathan Royal (who doubles on lead guitar and whistling), are at least on a par with many Swing Era band singers, which can be taken as rather faint praise. As for the orchestra, in terms of power and consonance, it is somewhere below the norm when compared to working professional ensembles, which the Hot House West orchestra does not claim to be. To verify that impression, one need do no more than listen to the closing number, Count Basie's classic "One O'Clock Jump." Case closed.

As no one is likely to amass much wealth performing with this group, it is assuredly a labor of love. And that is perhaps how it should be appraised—as a heartfelt summons to dancers and would-be dancers to leave the couch, head for a ballroom and immerse themselves in the irrepressible Joy of Rhythm.

Dark Eyes; Honeysuckle Rose; I'm Gonna Sit Right Down (And Write Myself a Letter); On the Sunny Side of the Street; Katusha; Grand Terrace Rhythm; I've Got Spurs (That Jingle, Jangle, Jingle); Hit That Jive Jack; A Mellow Bit of Rhythm; Them There Eyes; One O'clock Jump

items.body: One of our top albums of 2025 receives the remix treatment, as Hymnal (Resung) highlights six of the original fourteen tracks. Visionary vocalist Lyra Pramuk is well-served by these new takes, which highlight facets of the works that might otherwise have gone unnoticed. Sequenced in a different order, the EP rearranges our perceptions of the original set, which we preferred to play as a single extended piece. Only “Ending,” for obvious reasons, remains where it was. “Unchosen,” the second track on Hymnal, is now the opening piece. The original began with vibrating synth, while Tarta Relena Aspre begins with Pramuk’s voice, heard as if approaching from a corridor. While the pieces end in a similar place, the remix extends the sonic distance traveled in a much shorter span. In contrast, Pramuk more than doubles the length of “Reality,” which in its 2:17 form seemed more of a bridge track. Adding a new percussive framework, the artist creates what seems like an entirely different piece, with greater vocal separation. The moody, experimental “Meridian” gains beats and a dance floor sensibility from Laurel Halo and John Tejada. Could this be Pramuk’s first charted single? We hope so; the remix opens the artist to an entirely new audience. In like fashion, the beats arrived late in the original “Oracle,” but enter immediately in the “Verraco Weightless Reshape,” with propulsive drums and a half-speed breakdown. The string-laden “Swallow” stays pitched-down and mysterious under the direction of Dumama, a miasma of sound with stuttering spoken word, disintegrating in its final moments like a computer glitch. And while the original “Ending” cannot be topped, “Djrum’s Endless Rework” wisely goes the alternative route, operating under a completely different set of rules. Operating as a series of movements, the piece goes from percussive stormer to subdued sampler to tribal hypnotizer to nearly-a cappella blanket, as uncategorizable as Pramuk herself. While the rework is not actually “endless,” it suggests that there is no end to the talent of the artist or to her potential trajectory. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Broken rhythmic structures, exquisite sub-bass stutters, and destabilized funk mechanics colliding into something gloriously unhinged. It’s machine music with bloodstream heat—tactile, sensual, and absolutely devastating at volume. A four-track detonation of chrome-plated futurism whø’s latest transmission for Who Is Paula arrives like a preserved artifact from a parallel electro continuum where the 808 never stopped evolving and the 303 became an instrument of ecstatic machine hypnosis. Riding The Bassline is a four-track detonation of chrome-plated futurism, channeling the spirit of classic electro stylings through circuitry that feels simultaneously archival and startlingly alive. Every kick lands with pneumatic force, every bassline curls and mutates like liquid neon threading through a midnight motorway. The title track surges forward in a state of pure kinetic elevation, bubbling through synthetic cityscapes with elastic low-end pressure, celestial pads, and razor-edged drum programming that seems purpose-built for sweat-soaked dancefloor communion. We’ve only just started, and whø? simply doesn’t let up. “Voices” follows with a tougher mechanical stride before dissolving into waves of euphoric synth architecture and glowing harmonics that radiate outward like signals from some forgotten pleasure satellite. “Teebee Love” pivots toward a more eroticized strain of electro-funk, its grinding bass motif locking into a hypnotic body rhythm before erupting into a soaring string-pad climax of near-operatic intensity. Closing cut “I Can’t Get Enough Of That” pushes furthest into fractured territory: broken rhythmic structures, exquisite sub-bass stutters, and destabilized funk mechanics colliding into something gloriously unhinged. It’s machine music with bloodstream heat—tactile, sensual, and absolutely devastating at volume. Electron waves rise high.Paula‘s eyes half open, heart pounding, as she seeks the line, carving through the curving crown.And as the sine collapses she exits as one. Riding The Bassline is available on Who Is Paula. [Bandcamp] Riding The Bassline by whø? Who Is Paula · WIP011 – whø? – Riding The Bassline – Snippets

items.body: The waters here are torrid. But the result of swimming in them is to emerge somehow richer than before. The sound of subtraction through propulsion: the old and archaic riotously stripped away to leave space for the new. A violent recalibration disguised as transcendence. A fearsome and unrelenting expression of archetypal metallurgy Kotra drops Dim Ren as a fearsome and unrelenting expression of archetypal metallurgy channelling brutalist ancestral mores through a facade of the teachings of Odin. “Travellers” opens the three-piece with pulsating bandwidth of abrasive sonic weaponry. Full force and face melting. It’s to experience noise music as a psychedelic and hallucinatory bright light, where distortion itself becomes ceremonial and ecstatic rather than purely confrontational. “Loose Braids” traverses the same sonic landscape but seemed to evoke a propulsion of greens and golds through the inclusion of a deeper tectonic intent. Rhythms feel partially unearthed from beneath collapsing industrial strata, carrying an atmosphere of ritual circuitry and scorched acceleration. And closer “Wren Calibration” is a-typical industriana in warcry mode. If you are brave and adventurous then dive in. The waters here are torrid. But the result of swimming in them is to emerge somehow richer than before. The sound of subtraction through propulsion: the old and archaic riotously stripped away to leave space for the new. items.body: “Beautiful Patience” takes its name from sabr jamil, the patience Yaqub holds in the Quran when his son Yusuf is taken from him, across years, without complaint. Ghuraba الغرباء, the London duo of Mohammed Salih and Abdullah Mufa, build the track out of that. Salih plays electric guitar across Gnawa, Saharan blues and Anatolian modal territory, Mufa on the Ocean Drum, a frame drum filled with metal beads that roll across the skin. “Beautiful Patience” is one of the brighter tracks on Red Belly Robin, the duo’s second EP, released on 16 May, where Kazakh and Kyrgyz folk and a stray bluegrass lick open the vocabulary out from the heavier ground of 2025’s 6 Days. Both players are Muslim and work from inside the Sufi musical canon, and Salih has described the track as his reading of how the Yusuf story has shaped the way he sees the world. Stream “Beautiful Patience” and listen to Red Belly Robin via THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Ghuraba – الغرباء Beautiful Patience appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It was no coincidence that the band's name was inspired by the work "Rainbow in Curved Air" by minimalist composer Terry Riley. Nor was it a coincidence that their third album, Phantasmagoria, was named after Lewis Carroll's longest poem. A sequence of terrifying or fantastical, dreamlike images would undoubtedly help in visualizing the album's direction.Marie Antoinette...half ballad, half rock, driven by synthesizers, Sonja's voice (who also wrote many of the songs) sways like a hammock, gradually increasing in speed until it reaches a vertigo-inducing crescendo, amplified by the bass and guitar...before the tubular bells provide the necessary pause to further highlight the rock return in the song's second part. Another piece as complex as it is beautiful, a dreamlike work with which this journey begins, a fairy tale of yesteryear...the kind reminiscent of Andersen, who didn't shy away from darkness as part of the whole, in the ideal balance of art.Melinda (More or Less), with its harpsichord and guest flute by Annie Stewart, plus Darryl Way's violin, creates a medieval atmosphere that only deepens the sense of immersion in a fiction that grows ever more real. Sonja's vocals contrast with other registers, making her contribution all the more valuable. Not Quite the Same begins with trumpets reminiscent of the Renaissance, until the jazzy drums and Sonja's syncopated vocals bring it into the present, creating another instant classic for the group.Cheetah is an instrumental where Darryl Way's violin shines in all its splendor, and the virtuosity works in favor of the dramatic and emotional tension, something that is not so frequent, doing somersaults in the air, reaching low notes among all his high notes that make it deep and dark...with the drummer and bass following in his footsteps as if it were a frantic chase.More instant classics with the title track Phantasmagoria, where the organ, violin, and drums create a floating, ethereal, and light cloud where Sonja's voice travels, carrying forward those strange melodies that made Curved Air unique, half medieval, half avant-garde...The electronic experiments return in Whose Shoulder Are You Looking Over Anyway? , which serves as an introduction to "Over and Above." After a brief respite, the trumpets, violin, and keyboards return with full force at an accelerated pace, once again recalling the symphonic passages of Renaissance, when the band was one with the orchestra. Here, however, they are enhanced by the somewhat atonal compositions of Curved Air, which left them hanging on the cliff...visible and defiant like a flag in the middle of the mountain. Frank Ricotti on xylophone is fundamental to this track, along with the trumpets and trombones, which move from jazz to classical fugues...as if it were a new symphony for the new world. The Moog solo brings a new dimension, followed by the bass, which, together with the winds and xylophone, forms an orchestra that descends into the underworld before returning to pure tubular bell and distorted electric guitar.Once a Ghost, Always a Ghost closes with a jazzy calypso rhythm, which, while shifting the dramatic tension, serves as an awakening from that dream (at times a nightmare) established from the beginning.This is the classic Curved Air from the early days, the Francis Monkman era. Eddie Jobson would later arrive to fill in for the temporary departure of its founder, Daryl Way, but that's another story. The bonus track version includes Marie Antoinette sung in French, and it's not to be missed.

items.body: Review by AFlowerKingCrimson — This band has a sound that's rather hard to pin down. Overall, they are rather laid back and not very intense or heavy which can be a good thing if you just want something to relax to or at least something that is not metallish or too heavy. There are some elements that might bring to mind Pink Floyd and apparently on their subsequent albums there's a bit of a Dire Straits element (there's a little bit of that on here too but not much-mostly in some of the guitar sounds).Some of this has saxophone and there's also some flute, violin and cello. Also, much of this is rather "normal" sounding rock with maybe a bit of a roots rock or even a mild blues rock element (maybe that's where the Dire Straits comparisons come in). The first track, Pilgrim, which is in three secions is maybe the best thing on here but there are other fine moments as well. "From the Mist Rows the Bard" is nice also. However, I must say I'm not too keen on the fact that there are different lead vocalists on here and I'm especially not much of a fan of the singer with the rough raspy sounding voice. Just one singer and especially someone with a smoother voice would be more appreciated by me. Still, I wouldn't say it ruins the music and ultimately it's probably just a personal preference on my point. Overall, this is nothing earth shattering but it's a nice release. It's also rather short at 37 minutes and some change. It doesn't quite reach four stars for me but I'll give it 3.5. A nice album with some good Pink Floydish moments.

items.body: Review by uribreitman — An incredibly underrated blast from the not-so-distant past of (almost totally) instrumental prog. I would consider it a lost (almost lyrics-less) RUSH album from the late 70s, indeed.It has absolutely great trio-work, very similar to hard-prog outfits from the golden age.I love the fact that it doesn't follow any past convention, and just does whatever it wants.The most unique feature of the album (can't name it here, it's sooo long) that it isn't completely instrumental: The 11th track, "Halation", has some kind of sch-fi narration, which is very surprising but also highly evocative. Then it slides back to instrumental mode, like a theatrical finale closing, which is just what this album needs.To sum up this secret project, "Transmutations..." will appeal to RUSH fans which seek some mysterious and enigmatic music in their lives, while still hard-rocky and reflective. I find the lack of lyrics comforting and flat-out enjoyable. It's a shame that Maximum Indifference's (Mark, Rich and Gustaf) work met with, well - max global indifference. Recently I've found the album streaming safely on YouTube, so it's not totally gone.Give it a shot, and it'll grow on you like the old classics. I won't lie: It doesn't have the Neil Peart wise insights about the world, but it has plenty of melodic hooks, right-on riffs and brilliant ensemble playing. Clearly not essential listening, but excellent nonetheless.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Far from settling for the melodic formulas that defined much of the neo-prog of the 1980s and 1990s -and which they themselves had masterfully embodied- Pendragon took a bold turn towards rougher, more aggressive sounds -without, of course, losing sight of their sensitive DNA- with the daring "Believe" (2005). Three years later, they confirmed this evolution with the darker, more intense and instrumentally forceful "Pure" (2008), their eighth studio album.The muscular, overdriven guitar opening of the lengthy "Indigo" -arguably the album's finest track-, dramatised by distant dog barks, the psychedelia of its middle section built upon Clive Nolan's keyboards and Nick Barrett's two lengthy, enveloping solos -clearly Gilmourian in style- reflect the rockier path Pendragon chose to tread during the 2000s. A direction which, whilst keeping their neo-prog roots intact, introduces harder-edged riffs and magnetic atmospheres that bring the band closer to heavy prog territory, without quite reaching an industrial aesthetic, as can be heard in the furious "Eraserhead", the contemplative "Comatose I: View from the Seashore" or the energetic "The Freak Show".In a conceptual work that conveys a constant sense of unease, introspection and personal quest -epitomised by a troubled young contortionist unable to find meaning in his existence- the funkier and, at times, spacey "Comatose II: Space Cadet" and the mesmerising "Comatose III: Home and Dry" bring back the band's more melodic and crystalline side. Finally, the emotive arpeggiated ballad "It's Only Me", which drags on in its development, fails to blend naturally into the whole, partially blurring the concluding section of "Pure", an album that represented one of the rawest and most oppressive journeys in Pendragon's career.3.5 stars

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the most traditional flamenco sounding Spanish bands of the Rock Andaluz scene that tookSpain by storm in the late 70s and early 80s, the rather ridiculously named CAL that put out oneself-titled album with a rather bland and uninspiring album cover emerged from Seville's fertileflamenco rock scene following in the footsteps of Triana, Alameda and other predecessors. The lineupfeatured keyboardist and vocalist Alberto Toribio who was one of the pioneers of the style in theband Goma. Also along for the ride were Pepe Fern�ndez (guitar, vocals), Francisco Mu�oz (bass,vocals) and Juanjo Mu�oz (drums, vocals). Like many of the flamenco prog bands of the era, CAL (ironically there was another band at the timenamed Cai) took the world of flamenco and applied it to the context of symphonic prog but unlike thevibrant complexities of bands like Mezquita, Triana, Guadalquivir or Azahar, this band was mostlysteeped in its flamenco roots with the symphonic prog aspects providing a less dominant rolealthough the band made use of its share of mellotron, synthesizers and pianos with some moments ofnon-flamenco prog emerging along with the acoustic guitar, handclaps and castanets. Generallyspeaking the prog aspects are primarily used for intros and interludes while the flamenco partydominates the majority of the song structures.This album featured seven tracks running at about 35 minutes and primarily features rather simplecompositions that seem lazy and uninspired as much so as the rather ridiculous album cover art. Infact the whole thing feels like a frantic cash in while the Rock Andaluz boom was still hot. Whilethe music is a touch jazzier than most with fusion-like keyboards finding their way into the mix andsome extended song structures that qualify the album as bonafide progressive rock mostly in thelatter third of the album with tracks like "Ensayo En El Garbanzo" and the near 10-minute two-partcloser "Colgao" finally delivering the goods, overall it's a fairly insipidly weak affair with thatvibe of just barely getting the job done.No doubt about it, CAL was one of the weaker acts of the entire Rock Andaluz scene yet despite theband not really standing out in any particular way or sounding like what you would think eitherTriana or Alameda would sound like in demo form, the music isn't offensively banal or unlistenablein any way however in this fertile passionate micro-nook of the prog universe it just seems ratherbland and uninspiring and rather unessential in relation to some of the excellent bands that existedat the same time and considering that this band came from Seville, the Mecca of all things flamencoand cross-pollinating extensions, it sounds even less captivating! There isn't really anything ilike about this one. The band name is meh, the album cover is blah, the performances are mediocreand the compositors are ugh however it's still a good album as it delivers just enough spice to keepit from coming off as watered down gazpacho and even weak flamenco rock is still endearing to acertain degree.

items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — A band with a Tennessee vibe? Well, yes, because EVERSHIP hails from Nashville, a city better known for rock 'n' roll and bananas than for progressive rock! Yet it's from there that Shane Atkinson decided to send us his flagship album. Shane is a multi-instrumentalist composer who worked as a studio musician in the eighties and nineties, even composing commercials and film scores to make ends meet. After dabbling in the software industry, music haunted him so much that he decided to return to it, starting in 2005 with his own recording studio and equipment. The first compositions for the album presented here date back to 2009, so seven solid years to arrive at the remarkable result of this self-titled debut album.hane Atkinson handled almost all the instruments, with a few guest musicians including his own brother James on acoustic and lead guitars, and the invaluable vocal contribution of Beau West, an old childhood friend. And what vocals they are! From the very first track, "Silver Light," Freddie must be turning in his grave, so strongly does the song's emphasis evoke Queen, so powerfully operatic?an influence claimed (among others) by the master of ceremonies himself, the Queen of the pre-"News of the World" era, the very rock, frenetic Queen of the first five albums. The second track, "A Slow Descent Into Reality," takes us back to Liverpool in 1970 (and even earlier?), so strong is the influence of the Merseyside quartet in the opening. This is further enhanced by Queen's operatic feel, a touch of Kansas from Nicelle Priebe's violin, and a dash of classic Yes (the intricate bass lines and enchanting backing vocals). In short, a veritable who's who of the genre, all showcased by Shane Atkinson's multifaceted talent.And what can be said about the splendid "Evermore" that follows? Calm, delicate, and melodic (both divine and lyrical), with a magical piano, the electric guitar takes on a Bostonian character (though recapturing Tom Scholz's distinctive sound is no easy feat), and, as always, those majestic and magnificent backing vocals?a truly great moment of progressive rock. "Ultima Thule" continues in the same vein, a clear vocal tribute to our dearly departed Freddie and Brad in particular. Beau West establishes himself as an undeniable heir with his shimmering and delicate timbre, all sprinkled with a sublime violin in the finale. It's beautiful, it's wonderful...We thought we'd heard it all, but no! "Flying Machine" nails us to the delightful pillory of timeless progressive music. Our bliss and delight are unparalleled. The choirs, always the choirs (again, Boston, and also the entire musical spectrum of melodic rock from the last thirty years, not forgetting, on the other side of the Atlantic, the ever-popular Moody Blues), flood this track from beginning to end, and the orchestrations are simply fabulous.One minor point, but one that only concerns your reviewer: I didn't recognize the Theremin and Dulcimer that are supposed to be on the album. And a small criticism of this work: there's a lot of singing, but it's so well sung that forgiveness is in order.Another contender for the podium, a podium for which three steps won't be enough this year.Simply magnificent.Thank you, Mr. Atkinson.

items.body: Review by alainPP — 35 Tapes, sounds of the 70s, Genesis, Camel, and King Crimson. The studio band uses the 35 tapes as a reference point in the Mellotron, combining them with symphonic neo-prog."Hallway" is vintage pop-rock on period keyboards, hinting at the Crimson sound with its ethereal guitars. The rapid variation on the wooden piano evokes a solemn memory, the marshmallow guitar amplifying the meditative, nostalgic atmosphere. "Water" features languid Crimson-esque keyboards, Hackett-like guitar, a somber, melancholic air with hushed vocals, and a prominent bass reminiscent of Genesis's second era. The melting pot transforms into a musical axolotl, suspended between two worlds, with a melancholic finale. "Brise" combines soft keyboards and languid, contemplative vocal harmonies. The sound recalls Rick Miller's work with Hackett-style guitar, focusing on his psychic self etched in the mirror. A fusion of delicate, ever-evolving pop-rock sounds, a melancholic instrumental drift?the key word for this album. An ethereal, Genesis-esque, nostalgic, radiant finale."Borrowed Time" features a prominent bassline of symphonic prog rock, tearful and emotionally charged. The distant acoustic Greek guitar melody evokes the intense, charismatic atmosphere of Genesis, a magnified ersatz. A plaintive final guitar solo melts the listener's heart. "Clueless" is pop-rock with a rich vocal and a catchy, yet not over-the-top, rhythm. A touch of Canterbury lends itself to this meandering, timeless journey, allowing you to savor this vintage, cinematic moment. "Cities" opens with a melting, marshmallow-like guitar solo, a nostalgic beauty. The compressed melancholy recalls the aura of King Crimson, with vocals reminiscent of John. A shimmering piece poised between sadness and hope, the mystery of its composition blends numerous references to the 70s. The contained explosion, bass and organ intertwined for the keyboard finale on "Burning Rope," is fresh and joyful, filling the atmosphere with its energy.35 Tapes offers an immersion into misty realms where reality and imagination merge. Expect introspection, Mellotron, emotion, gentleness, and warmth.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — With members from bands I've already reviewed (Raccomandata Ricevuta Ritorno, Teoremi, and L'Uovo Di Colombo), Samadhi worked similarly to Il Volo, being a supergroup that leaned to the more pop aspects of Rock Progressivo Italiano. At only thirty five minutes long, I can definitely see room for improvement, but overall, a fine record that captures that more charming aspects of Italian prog at the time. It has a symphonic twinge that works well with the nature of the group, and though it can feel a little lackluster or uninspired, I can see a strong vision that came out as an okay project. The front cover also could've been more interesting other than just the simplistic design it holds. Moving on, among the players of the band, I overall enjoyed Luciano Regoli's vocals the most, as they fit the warm atmosphere of the music. The majority of the songs are all quite short, only being a few minutes long, but each of them has a nice whimsy to it that fills the area with a fun spirit. One thing I thought could've had more work was the production, as it feels a too hazy and it can come off as a little weak at points. My favorites from this album were the joyous and energized opener of Uomo Stanco, the quirky and sweet sound of L'Angelo, the cooler jam band vibes of Passaggio Di Via Arpino, and the longer more classically influenced L'Ultima Spiaggia, which also closes the record. On this album I could hear elements of what would later form into the sound of Maxophone, having that playful yet secretly quite intricate sound. On here, however, it can come off as feeling pretentious or that the band thinks they're doing something much more grand and greater than it actually is. Sure, it's good music with some pretty good high points here and there, but I wouldn't say it's life changing or anything. In conclusion, Samadhi is essentially just your run-of-the-mill Rock Progressivo Italiano record. Nothing mind-blowing, just some good tunes with some fine details sprinkled in. I'm thinking a strong 3.25/5 or a light 3.5/5 for this one.

items.body: Beim Duo Alan & Jan handelt es sich um die Produzenten und Klangkünstler Alan Abrahams, der unter anderem schon als Portable und Bodycode in Erscheinung trat, und Jan Jelinek, der seit über 25 Jahren seinen idiosynkratischen wie mikrotonalen Klangteppich knüpft und damit wohl ein eigenes Genre begründete. Take Me I’m Yours, die erste Zusammenarbeit der beiden, ist von der Cover-Art bis zum letzten Ton ein Collagen-Kunstwerk, wie es im Buche steht. Abrahams’ Songskizzen und verschiedenste Vokalspuren schickte dieser für einen Manipulations- und Produktionsprozess der besonderen Art an Jelinek, dessen abstraktes elektronisches Sounddesign sehr gut als Kontrapunkt zum organischen Klang der Stimme funktioniert. Mal geht Jelinek dabei recht rigoros vor und verfremdet die Stimme bis zur Unkenntlichkeit oder pitcht sie auf Zeitlupe herunter (»Together«). An anderer Stelle wird Alans Stimme zu gespenstischen Chorälen gelayert wie in »Window (Elpis)«. Im frühen Album-Highlight »Forever« hört man sogar eine nahezu klassische Gesangsperformance, inklusive Melodie und Text. Meist sampelt Jelinek aber nur für Sekundenbruchteile und benutzt Abrahams’ Stimme als organische Klangquelle, aus der er dann selbst kleine Melodien, Flächen und sanft pulsierende Beats bastelt. Abstrakt und doch geerdet entsteht auf Take Me I’m Yours aus vielen kleinen, subtilen Sounds ein großes Gesamtbild, das zwischen den zwei Welten von Alan und Jan vermittelt – und dabei eine dritte entstehen lässt.

items.body: Bei Human Space Machine handelt es sich nicht um den nervigen Ellenbogen-Proleten auf dem Dancefloor, sondern um einen niederländischen Techno-Act. Er würde wohl kaum auf Midgar erscheinen, wenn sich seine Musik nicht an der Grenze zur Klangforschung bewegen würde. Soll heißen: Auch die EP Perception Field ist selten nur vorwärts gedacht, sondern beweist ein Gespür für die feinen Zwischentöne, die Maschinenmusik ermöglicht. Psychedelik, Hall, das böse Wort Tribalismus? Der dahingehend betitelte Track »Totem« sediert trotz seines vergleichsweise hohen Tempos mit organischen Geräuschen aus anorganischer Materie, hallt wie jener See, aus dem Donato Dozzy und Neel eine Klangsignatur für die Ewigkeit schufen. Auch der Opener »The Field« weist eine gewisse Geschwindigkeit auf, entwickelt aber die eigenwillige Gangart einer fiebrigen Reagenzglasgeburt im Ambient-Deckmantel. Auf »U77« dengeln über moderater Geschwindigkeit metallene Glockenschläge relativ klar, obwohl man sich auf der Turmwendeltreppe immer weiter bergab in die Dunkelheit begibt, ein Track gewordenes Castlevania mit komplementären Basseinsätzen. »Gallop« ballert polyrhythmisch auf Höchstgeschwindigkeit und lullt dabei mit Glockenspielereien ein. Tech-House-Anwandlungen in Bass-Music-Ästhetik wie bei Wisdom Teeth, fulminant durchexerziert. Konzeptionell der gelungenste Track einer EP, die vieles ist, aber sicherlich keine Gebrauchsmusik.

items.body: Athens duo Incirrina have released the album “Trace” on the German label Cold Transmission Music. The Incirrina “Trace” album runs to 11 tracks and follows the duo’s two previous albums, “8.15” (2019) and “Lip Led Scream” (2022). The band describe “Trace” as built around freedom, identity and resistance. The 11 tracks were written between 2023 and 2025 and recorded through a 24-channel console, using analogue electronic instruments and the duo’s vocals. The album follows “Lip Led Scream” (2022), the duo’s first record for Cold Transmission Music. “Trace” is issued on vinyl (black and crystal-clear), CD, a limited cassette and digital. “Mutate” and “Always Here” were released as advance singles, and “Mutate” has an accompanying video on YouTube. The album is available through Cold Transmission Music (coldtransmission.com) and the band’s Bandcamp. Trace by Incirrina About Incirrina Incirrina is a dark electronic and minimal synth duo based in Athens, Greece, formed in late 2017 by George Katsanos (synthesizers, drum machine, waterphone, vocals) and Irini Tiniakou (synthesizers, vocals). The duo describe their work as “dark, poetic, electronic,” pairing analogue synth lines and drum-machine rhythms with Tiniakou’s vocals. Tiniakou first appeared as a guest vocalist on a release by the Greek act Metal Disco before Incirrina became a project in its own right. The duo debuted with the album “8.15” (2019, Geheimnis Records), a record drawing on the work of the 18th-century poet William Blake. They followed it with the digital maxi-single “Utter” (2020) and a 2021 split maxi-single with The Man & His Failures, “Devastations / R.Daneel,” on Smash Records. Their second album, “Lip Led Scream” (2022), was their first release for Germany’s Cold Transmission Music, which has handled their releases since. In 2024 they released the double single “Immersion” (“Presence” and “Alien Room”), also on Cold Transmission Music. In an April 2023 Side-Line reviewer Inferno Sound Diaries described “Lip Led Scream” as “a pure Cold-Wave production which is sometimes reinforced with harder, EBM, elements” and as “a well-crafted and fully enjoyable work without any single cut to throw away,” rating it 8/10. The duo have performed in Greece, Germany, Belgium, Hungary and Croatia, with festival appearances at Plíísken Festival, Morphic Festival, Cold Transmission Festival. Death Disco Festival – The Warm Up, Athens Music Week, Metavasis Festival and the Athens Digital Arts Festival. “Trace,” their third album, is their latest release for Cold Transmission Music.

items.body: Steve Roach‘s “Quiet Music” series, originally recorded between 1983 and 1986 and released on Projekt Records, will be available on vinyl for the first time as a complete 3LP set. The Steve Roach “Quiet Music” 40th Anniversary edition is pressed on three ultra clear 140g LPs in a limited edition of 300 copies, and will be out August 7, 2026 so Audioglobe informs. The set collects all three original “Quiet Music” albums in one outer sleeve with black paper inner sleeves and a two-sided credits insert. The pressing is 140g ultra clear vinyl, limited strictly to 300 copies. The full tracklist across the three LPs is as follows. “Quiet Music 1”: A1 “The Green Place, Part I” (24:44); B1 “The Green Place, Part II” (24:52). “Quiet Music 2”: A1 “See Things” (5:45); A2 “Towards the Blue” (3:20); A3 “Something in Tears” (5:18); A4 “A Few More Moments” (13:05); B1 “Air and Light” (25:51). “Quiet Music 3”: A1 “Dreaming and Sleep” (18:16); A2 “Quiet Canon” (7:28); B1 “Sleep and Dreaming” (24:47). Quiet Music by Steve Roach Here’s what Steve Roach says on “Quiet Music” at 40 years: “In looking at the arc of my music, 40 years after creating Quiet Music,” Roach stated in the release materials, “I still feel an unbroken connection to this same inner breath and pulse I was discovering within myself and my creative life at that time. Even with everything that was going on in the early ’80s — musically, culturally, politically — this music came to exist in its own dimension, outside of that time, separate from the day-to-day climate in which I was surrounded. I was yearning to express a timeless and universal soul-tone, a safe haven within the music.” Composer Harold Budd said this when the release first came out in 1986: “I think Steve Roach’s Quiet Music is his best album. It’s not that it’s simply pretty (which it is), but there’s an odd edge lurking in the background that moves it miles away from ‘New Age’ torpor. This is a lovely album from a composer working at the top of his skills.” About Steve Roach Steve Roach is an American composer and performer born in 1955, based in Tucson, Arizona. He began working with synthesizers in the early 1980s and established an international reputation through recordings released on Projekt Records, among other labels. His 1984 album “Structures from Silence” – reissued on its third vinyl edition by Projekt in April 2025 – is considered a foundational work of ambient music. The “Quiet Music” series originated in commissions for healing-arts programmes and was released on cassette in 1986; the recordings draw on synthesizers, flute, electric piano and natural sounds. Roach has continued releasing new studio and live work at high frequency; Our most recent coverage concerned the limited 2CD live release “La Rosa — Live in Tucson, 2025” in May 2026. The “Quiet Music” 3LP set, out August 7, 2026, marks the first time the complete series has been issued on vinyl in a single edition.

items.body: Norwegian solo artist Chris Wicked releases a gothic rock and dark synthpop cover of Depeche Mode‘s “Enjoy the Silence” on June 2, 2026, via Raven Black Productions. The Bergen-based artist here mixes gothic, cinematic and alternative rock. This is the third single from his forthcoming EP “Black Horns & Black Hooves.” Chris Wicked explains his reasons for choosing the song: “Enjoy the Silence has always been a song that resonated with me. The atmosphere, the sense of longing and the timeless darkness within the melody have inspired me since I was young. We didn’t want to copy the original — we wanted to reinterpret it through our own musical universe.” The cover arrives as the third single from the upcoming EP “Black Horns & Black Hooves” on Raven Black Productions. It follows “Utan Dina Andetag,” a cover of a Kent track released in December 2024 as the first single from the project, and “Wicked Game,” a cover of the Chris Isaak song released in September 2025 as the second single. About Chris Wicked Chris Wicked is a solo artist from Bergen, Norway. He came to wider attention as the founder and vocalist of Malice In Wonderland, a Norwegian rock band formed in the late 1990s before releasing a debut album and single “Lucifer’s Town” in 2005. Musically Malice In Wonderland’s sound combines glam, goth and hard rock elements. The band toured across Europe and Asia, sharing stages with acts including Def Leppard, and appeared in television productions. Their final album, “The Royal Brigade,” was released in December 2013, mixed by John Fryer, known for his work with Depeche Mode and Nine Inch Nails. In August 2015, Malice In Wonderland announced their break-up and completed a series of farewell shows in Norway and abroad. Chris Wicked subsequently announced a solo career, recording under his own name. His debut solo album, “Aleine,” was released in 2021 via Apollon Records and featured guest appearances from Gaahl (Gorgoroth), Hoest (Taake), Niklas Kvarforth (Shining) and V’gandr (Helheim). In 2024, he released the dark Nordic folk single “Northern Heart” on Raven Black Productions. Malice In Wonderland returned in 2025 to mark the 20th anniversary of their 2005 debut, releasing new and reimagined material including “I’ve Chosen Darkness (Over You)” and a revisited edition of “Lucifer’s Town” in 2025, followed by the single “Dying Breed” in 2026.

items.body: Cold Spring Records has announced a vinyl repress of Trepaneringsritualen’s “Perfection & Permanence” death industrial LP, due June 12, 2026. The edition is pressed on moss green vinyl, limited to 500 copies. The original LP was released in 2014 and has been out of print for nearly a decade. The repress replicates the original 2014 LP programme in full across two sides. Side A: “Venerated & Despised” (2:34), “A Black Egg” (3:54), “Castrate Christ” (4:37), “Liken Ingen Jord Vill Svälja” (2:34), “Alone/A/Cross/Abyss” (3:48). Side B: “Thirty-Nine Lashes” (2:37), “The Seventh Man” (3:24), “Konung Krönt I Blod” (3:30), “A Ceaseless Howling” (3:29), “He Who Is My Mirror” (5:17). Perfection & Permanence by Trepaneringsritualen About Trepaneringsritualen Trepaneringsritualen is a death industrial and ritual ambient project founded by Swedish artist Thomas Martin Ekelund in 2008, initially based in Göteborg, Sweden, and later relocating to Berlin, Germany. The project released its first full-length, “Deathward, to the Womb”, in 2012 on Cold Spring Records. Side-Line reviewed the album at the time of release. “Perfection & Permanence” followed in 2014 on the same label, issued simultaneously on CD and LP; the white vinyl LP edition was limited to 500 copies. In 2017, Trepaneringsritualen released the full-length “Kainskult” on Tesco Organisation, and the project also collaborated with MZ.412 on the live document “Post Industriale / Rituals” 2LP. The same year, the project compiled two earlier split LPs on the CD “Yours Is a Kingdom of Death”. In 2018, Trepaneringsritualen and Nordvargr released “Alpha Ænigma”, a collaborative album. The project subsequently appeared on Cold Spring’s compilation “Arise – A Cold Spring Sampler” in 2023. In 2021, Thomas Martin Ekelund partnered with Henrik Nordvargr Björkk on “Lidaverken Del I: Att i Vådeld Förgås”. The project has released further albums including “ᛉᛦ – Algir; eller Algir i Merkstave” (2019) and “The Totality of Death (A)” and “The Totality of Death (Ω)” (both 2024). The repress of Trepaneringsritualen “Perfection & Permanence” is available via Cold Spring Records.

items.body: Denver project Neo Dimes has released “Alone,” a ten-track debut full-length album spanning darkwave, neo-industrial, alternative rock and synthpop. The album arrived on vinyl and cassette on May 19, 2026, with the digital release scheduled later this month later. Neo Dimes is the solo project of Denver-based musician Stephen Edmunds. “Alone” addresses digital-age isolation, algorithmic control, surveillance capitalism, online extremism and the experience of aging into a world shaped by technology. The record mixes neo-industrial, alternative rock, darkwave and synthpop. Alone by Neo Dimes The album’s artwork is built around a visual narrative: each of the ten single covers functions as a chapter, representing themes of paranoia, persuasion, control and acceptance, which combine to form the final album cover. Edmunds commented as follows on the album’s intent: “I recently lost a career right as my daughter came into the world — a world where she has fewer rights than her mother did and where tyranny is creeping into every facet of life. We’re addicted to the technology in our pockets that opens us to the world by consuming us entirely. It’s omnipresent and inescapable, and I’m pissed off.” Several tracks were released as singles ahead of the album. “Beasts” addresses what Edmunds describes as the radicalization of young men in the wake of the collapse of the American dream. “Angels” casts digital connectivity and surveillance as a modern substitute for guardianship. “Don’t Think” addresses manufactured consent and propaganda. “Trigger” connects personal experiences of addiction, anxiety and isolation. Note that a music video for “Trigger,” directed by Ty Borkowski, was also released. About Neo Dimes Neo Dimes is the solo project of Stephen Edmunds, a Denver, Colorado-based musician. Edmunds has spent most of his life as a musician, starting with guitar in hardcore and metal bands before moving into shoegaze and experimental music. The Neo Dimes project developed over approximately seven years, during which Edmunds worked through the production and compositional process largely through self-teaching. The project made its first public appearance in late 2024, when Edmunds contributed a remix of “Careful What You Wish For” by Highlands. The first original Neo Dimes material appeared in late 2025, with the single “Angels” released on October 30, 2025, followed by “Beasts” on December 9, 2025. Further singles, including “Don’t Think,” preceded the album’s release. Edmunds cites Nine Inch Nails, Depeche Mode and Deftones as primary influences, with The Cure, Joy Division, Brian Jonestown Massacre, My Bloody Valentine and The Prodigy also cited as formative references. “Alone” is the first full-length release under the Neo Dimes name.

items.body: French duo Potochkine‘s 2025 album “Sang d’Encre” is back in a second limited vinyl pressing on the young & cold label Audioglobe informs us. The new edition is limited to 333 copies on grey splatters vinyl. The first vinyl edition of “Sang d’Encre,” issued in late 2025, was pressed on red transparent with black marble vinyl. The current pressing uses grey splatters vinyl. Both pressings are limited to 333 copies. The album is also available on CD and digital. Sang d'Encre by POTOCHKINE “Sang d’Encre” holds seven tracks: “Bi,” “Endorphines,” “Partir,” “Tristesse Fantasmée,” “Bonnie,” “Pénurie de Larmes,” and the closing ambient piece “La Source.” Two tracks have accompanying videos: “Bi” and “Endorphines”. About Potochkine Potochkine is a French dark electronic duo formed in Paris in 2016, composed of vocalist Pauline Alcaïdé and producer Hugo Sempé. The pair built their sound around French-language vocals, electronic rhythms and a production approach drawing on EBM, electro and elements of darkwave and coldwave. The duo’s debut was the EP “Libérez votre imagination” (2016), which introduced their combination of dark electronics and theatrical staging. They followed with the self-titled album “Potochkine” (2018) and “Mythes” (2019), before releasing “Sortilèges” in 2021 on young & cold – their first release for the German label. A remix companion, “Sortilèges dans le club,” also appeared in 2021. The single “Endorphines” was released in 2024 ahead of “Sang d’Encre.” “Sang d’Encre” was released in autumn 2025 on young & cold as Potochkine’s fourth studio album and their second record for the label. The second vinyl pressing, on grey splatters vinyl, is available now through the young & cold webshop and its distribution network via Audioglobe.

items.body: Tomasz Lukowicz has already earned his stripes with his Fractal project, through which he has released a truckload of productions. With Replicant, he reveals another side of his skills, and on the debut album “Critical Point”, he delivers 11 compelling tracks. Replicant sounds very different — more like an experiment in which the operator takes us deep into his sonic laboratory, completely unleashing his creativity in sound design. He supports these experiments with slow rhythms and broken beats. Lukowicz reveals himself here as a true sound architect, showcasing an impressive sonic landscape. I particularly enjoy the depth he creates in his bass lines, as well as some of the space-like electro arrangements. The whole album remains entirely instrumental. A touch of vocals or sampling here and there would not have felt out of place, but “Critical Point” already stands firmly on its own. The album even contains a few minimalist gems that are simply impossible to ignore. This is the kind of release that would have appealed to fans of the Tympanik Audio label back in the day, but which has now found the right home on Aliens Production. Call it Experimental with a touch of IDM subtlety, or simply Electro freestyle — this debut album is certainly an intriguing discovery. (Rating:8). Listen to “Depressing Fate Of Humanity”: https://aliensproduction.bandcamp.com/track/depresing-fate-of-humanity

items.body: If you want to be countedIf you want to be seenThen you can never be freeNot me Black Marble, the long-running solo project of synth musician Chris Stewart, will return this summer with Life in Small Spaces, his first full-length album since 2021’s Fast Idol. The record is due on August 21, 2026, via Sacred Bones, and its announcement comes with a new single, “Jim Carol New Year,” alongside a 16mm video directed by Clayton Hunt. The title carries a sly double meaning, nodding to author, poet, and musician Jim Carroll while brushing against the sing-song formality of holiday carols. The song itself is less festive than the name suggests, though it moves with a dry, almost buoyant touch. Stewart sets a rhythmic synth figure against a clipped, cool vocal delivery, letting the track drift between deadpan humour and a serious suspicion of authority, belief, approval, and all the social traps dressed up as advice. Jim Carol New Year casts a skeptical eye on the voices that claim authority over modern life: teachers, preachers, critics, experts, and anyone else selling certainty as salvation. Stewart turns the repeated phrase “I forgot my money” into a dry punchline and a philosophical dodge, as if the speaker has wandered into the marketplace of bad advice and left his wallet at home on purpose. The song treats public approval, easy belief, and social belonging as traps dressed up as rewards, while its brighter melodic movement gives the critique a sly lift. Beneath the humour sits a more personal bruise, with failed intimacy and self-recognition slipping into the frame, deepening the song’s argument about freedom, compromise, and the cost of being seen. “If you want to be free,” Stewart says, “you have to watch out for some of life’s classic pitfalls.” Black Marble has a gift for making private unease feel oddly aerodynamic, and Stewart applies that instinct to a song about doubt as self-preservation. The arrangement glides with a melody that carries the critique in clean lines instead of forcing the point. Its charm works as camouflage for a tougher thought: the desire to be recognized can become its own quiet trap. “Chris had an idea of a house in the distance with two travelers being drawn toward it,” director Clayton Hunt shares regarding the video. “We wanted each traveler to represent a different version of the journey. One traveler struggled unprotected against the landscape, the other was cautious, outfitted in an orange hazmat – type suit. I decided to shoot 16mm and capture everything against the green landscape, creating a vibrant contrast. That imagery helped guide the production and inform the story.” Hunt’s video gives the single a spare, strange visual frame. Rather than crowding the song with plot, the clip follows two travelers drawn toward a distant house. One moves exposed through the open landscape, while the other proceeds with caution in an orange hazmat-type suit. The image is simple enough to read in several directions: risk and protection, instinct and fear, faith and armor, two ways of moving toward the same uncertain promise. The 16mm format suits Black Marble’s current turn toward a more physical band-room feel. Watch the video for Jim Carol New Year below: Black Marble’s Life in Small Spaces finds Stewart trading some of his usual synth density for staccato guitar lines inspired by early American left-of-the-dial college radio, with reference points including Pylon, The Necessaries, and R. Stevie Moore. Live drum samples, informed by Wire’s clean metronomic economy, help shift the project toward a leaner, more tactile sound. Stewart describes the album as a record about the music industry, authenticity, and the question of how independent artists survive without surrendering the private logic that made the work worth making in the first place. “I always knew a lot of people in music struggled to make ends meet, but it surprised me to learn that the people you thought would be doing well often weren’t. For me, seeing the business from the inside like that changed how I looked at things. When I looked up to see a new artist on a billboard, I started to wonder, will I one day have to pretend to be something I’m not, in order to succeed? The life of an artist goes on after your moment ends, you know? So who do you want to be in the end and how do you want to be seen by the people that know you? I made Life In Small Spaces while thinking about that, and for me, it serves as my own ideal for living an artistic life. I’m doing it as a vocation, not some last ditch effort to escape to some other world. I made this record not only as a way of saying that, but as a way of saying it’s ok to feel that way. It’s ok for people to sacrifice some degree of creature comfort in order to live a life you believe in. And it doesn’t have to be an endless search for something just out of reach, it can be a permanent way of being and something that sustains you.” In that sense, Jim Carol New Year makes for a pointed first dispatch. Its melody may turn lightly, but its message keeps its composure: beware the expert, distrust the sales pitch, and save your freedom for something worth more than being seen. items.body: Puerta Negra’s latest single Complejo de Victima (Victim Mentality), comes on as a scathing indictment delivered with immaculate control. It’s strict, stylish, and wired for confrontation. Here, the Portland duo of María Aguirre and Mark Arciaga treat body music as a blunt instrument with a brain attached to it, and this lead single from their Metafísica EP sharpens the blade without polishing away any vitriol. Sung entirely in Spanish, the track places Aguirre’s voice at the center of the damage, cool and cutting, while the beat lurches forward with the mechanical confidence of a machine trained on human spite. Musically, Complejo de Victima works from a lean EBM chassis and lets the parts rattle. Industrial funk pressure runs through the track, but it never loosens into party decoration. The electronics have a mutant bite, closer to a feverish factory floor than a club fantasy, while the broken rhythms keep shoving the body forward at odd angles. Oráculo references Cabaret Voltaire, new-beat mutations, and the contemporary EBM revival, showcasing themselves as a band pushing their musical heritage through clenched teeth. Directed by Zach Flanary, the official video keeps its world deliberately stripped down: black-and-white, high contrast, bodies under pressure, faces treated less as glamour objects than as evidence. Aguirre and Arciaga perform as if trapped inside the song’s own nervous system, caught between command and collapse. The mirror shots give the video its mean little genius. They bend the performance into something fractured without dragging it into cheap psychodrama. A face splits, a figure doubles, the eye gets tricked into watching the watcher, and the victim complex named in the title starts to feel less like a diagnosis than a room full of bad faith. There is no need for plot when the premise is already poisoned: accusation, self-pity, control, and the private theater people build around their own wounds. Watch the video for Complejo de Victima below: Metafísica is billed as the third chapter in Puerta Negra’s vision, following 2022’s Costo Humano and 2023’s Playa Sola, and Complejo de Victima feels like a hard pivot toward austerity, attack, and psychic compression. Severity can be seductive when handled with nerve. Listen to Complejo de Victima below and pre-order the vinyl (out June 12th from Oráculo Records) here. items.body: In Anthology, the debut EP by Glaswork, Joshua Elijah makes a departure from the sharper angles of his previous work with Inertia Her, entering a more severe, spacious register. The Paris-based artist, producer, mixing engineer, and photographer has carried over a certain discipline from his earlier work, but the gesture here is one of subtraction rather than expansion. Across five tracks, Glaswork strips song form down to pressure, pulse, and pallor, allowing ambient electronics, contemporary classical texture, and EBM-derived movement to meet in a place where precision becomes emotional. The record has the feel of architecture abandoned before occupancy: corridors of tone, low mechanical thuds, rooms implied by resonance rather than filled with ornament. Elijah’s use of analogue and digital processes gives the music a tactile instability, as if each sound were being handled while still warm from the machine. There are traces of Tim Hecker’s engulfing grain and CoH’s sleek austerity, but Glaswork’s instincts are more private, less grandly apocalyptic. He works in measured gestures, allowing a bass figure or a softened industrial pulse to appear, recede, and leave behind a kind of charged absence. “Anthology is the result of mixing analogue and digital processes and letting experimentation lead the way,” says Elijah. “…five tracks built from dark electronic textures, ambient space, and restrained rhythmic ideas, focused more on mood and atmosphere than structure.” The statement points to the EP’s central temperament. These pieces do not hurry toward resolution. They collect and disperse, gathering weight through proximity. A rhythm may suggest the body, but it rarely gives itself over to club logic; a synth line may gesture toward melody, then dissolve into a colder field of tone. Elijah seems uninterested in spectacle, choosing instead to let small details carry the burden of feeling: the grain at the edge of a drone, the blunt knock of a beat, the way a suspended note can seem to alter the scale of the room around it. The EP’s emotional force lies in that refusal of excess. Glaswork begins here as a project of concentration, one concerned with the drama of reduction, where darkness is measured, space is active, and silence becomes another instrument in the arrangement. Listen to Anthology below and pre-order the album here. items.body: Re:Mission Entertainment has signed somemagicalshit, the bilingual synthpop and dark electronic project of Houston’s Courtnii Veronica Rose, with a debut full-length album set for release this fall. The announcement gives a proper label frame to a project already wired for bruised nerves, bad glamour, private panic, and the kind of synth damage that makes a bedroom feel like a pirate radio broadcast tower. Rose started somemagicalshit in 2022 as a solo operation: computer, synths, sequencers, and a skull full of voltage. By 2023, the project had grown into a full live band, which makes sense, because this is the kind of music that wants bodies dancing in front of it. It has Le Tigre’s art-damaged bite, TR/ST’s bruised electronic glamour, ADULT.’s stern machine-body snap, Pussy Riot’s bilingual agit-pop provocation, and the frostbitten drama of Kælan Mikla, all dragged through Rose’s own Houston heat and private hell. She writes, records, mixes, and directs the entire affair herself, building songs that feel glossy, unstable, wounded, and ready to throw a drink at the mirror. Я ненавижу себя moves between Russian and English as Rose calls herself ugly, rejects advice, declares therapy useless, reaches for alcohol as medicine, and circles the same brutal thought until it becomes a chorus: “Ya Nenavizyu Sebya.” The title translates to “I Hate Myself,” and the track treats that phrase with the blunt force of a diary entry written hard enough to tear the page. There’s face paint, jealousy, body disgust, and the desperate wish to love herself again, all carried by stacked synthesizers and vocals that cut through the arrangement with theatrical ache. The Russian lyrics give somemagicalshit a serrated emotional edge, bending the song’s pain into something harsher, stranger, and more intimate than plain English confession could manage alone. Rose’s voice moves from sneer to exposed nerve without getting coy about the damage, while the music keeps enough pop instinct to make the misery stick in your teeth. “The goal from the beginning was to create something atmospheric and emotionally intense while incorporating the beauty and emotion of the Russian language into alternative electronic music,” says Rose. “That mission hasn’t changed. It’s only getting louder.” The video for Я ненавижу себя, directed by Jorge Delgado, turns self-loathing into a public spectacle with a weird grin taped to its face. Rose performs with live-wire force while an audience watches from behind paper bag masks, reflecting the song’s shame. The clip has the charge of a basement show, a breakdown, and a prank pulled on the bad voice in your head all at once. “This is a song about suffering with self-hatred, making this video was a dream come true for me and I hope that you all enjoy it! It is slightly humorous as well as serious,” says Rose. Watch below: Houston’s alternative scene has already been getting the message, with short tours, out-of-town dates, and new material pushing the project beyond its original bedroom-bunker beginnings. With Re:Mission now behind it, somemagicalshit’s forthcoming full-length looks set to deliver a very stylish nervous breakdown with teeth. Catch somemagicalshit on the road in the America South this summer! June 5, 2026 The Crypt, New Orleans, LA w/ Blood Lovely, Phoenix Phantasma July 10, 2026 The Mix, San Antonio, TX w/ Shelly Webster + more TBA August 28, 2026 Crow Bar (Raven Room), Houston, TX w/ In The Shadows, Andrako, DJ Whisperwish Discover more from Re:Mission Entertainment here, and check out their official Bandcamp page here. items.body: Kurs Murder (P. 1) Swiss Dark Nights One-man Italian act Kurs has had both its musical aesthetic and a unique approach to LP release locked in from its 2021 debut, and isn’t deviating from that approach the third time out. As with preceding Kurs records, Murder (P. 1) isn’t just a concept record in and of itself but also ships with a graphic novel fleshing that concept out. Lacking said book we can only presume that this is intended as the first volume of an ongoing series of records/books, but you don’t need that larger context in order to appreciate Valerio Rivieccio’s yen for moody and stormy electro-industrial. Kurs remains a project which rewards focused headphone listening rather than club fodder hunting, and the loping rhythmic slither and numbly distorted hums on lead single “Weapon” are a great demonstration of why we’ve been waiting so keenly for Kurs’ next move. The ebb and flow of the track’s build and release is considered and never rushed, building towards churning drums and acidic vocals, but along the way there’s much in the way of satisfying and finely textured programming that’s catnip to the seasoned rivethead. Those moves don’t just take the form of traditionally noisy elements, either; opener “Precinct” gradually expands in scope, pulling back from the minimal, chilly EBM pulse of its first moments into a more cinematic mode framed by horns. As always, Kurs is a project whose roots are easy to spot if one cares to look for them, but Murder (P. 1) never comes up short even in that sort of perspective. The influence Front Line Assembly has on Kurs, which has always been detectable in the corners of the preceding records, becomes more apparent on a number of pieces here, as on the Leeb-esque chorus of “Murder” and on the galloping programming of “Basement” which treads the line between martial bombast and pure clattering chaos. Lifts like that don’t necessarily hit the most overt aesthetic or musical cues other bands have taken from FLA, though, and as with preceding LPs Muter and Dreamer so much work has gone into building up Kurs’ own world of sound and atmosphere that these moments (or the occasional parallel with mid-period Haujobb) feel like tips of the hat and never overt coattail riding. The imagery conjured by Murder (P. 1)‘s titles and lyrics are plenty evocative even sans accompanying text, and it’s easy to build a Deus Ex or Dark City inspired landscape in your mind’s eye as you listen. If that all sounds like nostalgia for cyber-dystopias of the past rather than the one we’re living in, fair enough, but once again Kurs have put so much work into their craft that the histories they’re drawing upon soon fade from the listener’s mind as they enjoy Kurs qua Kurs. Buy it. Murder (P. 1) by Kurs The post Kurs, “Murder (P. 1)” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
